Mr. Speaker, according to a report made public today by Statistics Canada, the housewives of this nation by their work earn approximately $80 billion a year and are responsible for about 40 per cent of the gross national product. It seems to me that it is time we did something about this, but I suppose if 1 suggested that the bill be paid, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) would have a heart attack. We could start, however, by establishing pension equality for women. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent):
That this House calls on the government to recognize the contribution that women in their homes make to our economy and, as a minimum, to recognize this contribution by establishing pension equality, including the equivalent of the Canada Pension Plan for women whose work is in their homes, equal pension rights for all women between the ages of 60 and 65 regardless of marital status, increasing the pensions paid to widows under various government plans to at least 75 per cent, and the continuing payment of pensions granted to widows regardless of any subsequent change in marital status.

Millhaven penitentiary authorities recently decided that as of June 19 last all visits in a common hall for inmates in special units, that is inmates escorted by guards, would be reduced from seven days a week to a single day-Tuesday. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a matter of personal privilege of which I have given you notice. I understand that this afternoon this House will consider a government motion in relation to the Constitution of Canada. In recent days I have studied and carefully examined the government's proposals as set out in the white paper called "A Time for Action", and in the constitutional amendment bill, Bill C-60, which was given first reading in the House last week.
I am convinced from studying those documents that this government legislation cannot possibly achieve unity in this country. In fact I find myself in such fundamental disagreement with the government's proposals that I can no longer, in good conscience, sit on the government side of the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister) moved:
speechtext:
That a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons be appointed to examine and report upon proposals that have been made and in the future are from time to time made public by the Government of Canada, on subjects related to the Constitution of Canada;
That twenty Members of the House of Commons, to be designated by the House at a later date, be members of the said committee on the part of this House;
That the committee have power to examine and enquire into all such matters as may be referred to them by the House, and to report from time to time, and, except when the House otherwise orders, to send for persons, papers and records, to sit while the House is sitting, to sit during periods when the House stands adjourned, to print from day to day such papers and evidence as may be ordered by them, and to delegate to sub-committees all or any of their powers except the power to report direct to the House;
That the committee have power to adjourn from place to place within Canada; and
That a message be sent to the Senate requesting their Honours to unite with this House for the above purpose, and to select, if the Senate deems so advisable, some of its members to act on the proposed Special Joint Committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, to say the least, at the outset of this debate, the constitutional issue has been with us for a long time. It is in 1927 that efforts were initiated, under the government of my predecessor, William Lyon Mackenzie King, some time between the Balfour Declaration and the Statute of Westminster, of 1931, those two steps which enabled Canada, formerly a colony, to accede formally and legally to the status of an independant country.
1 shall not refer to the intermediate steps-there were many-but 1 shall deal briefly with the last stage which started in 1967, this time on the initiative of the provinces, when Mr. Robarts, the then Ontario premier, convened the so-called Confederation of Tomorrow Conference, which was followed soon after by a series of federal-provincial meetings at the first minister level, the first of which was called in February 1968 by my illustrious predecessor, Mr. Lester B. Pearson.
The Constitution
This last stage, which extended over a period of several years, saw the publication of many white papers which were debated at various federal-provincial conferences, which resulted in a complete failure at the so-called Charter of Victoria Conference in 1971. The Victoria effort, however, was partly brought back to life between 1975 and 1977 both at meetings and through an exchange of correspondence between the premiers and myself, where we considered the possibility of implementing a number of clauses of the Victoria Charter.
In view of this long series of failures which has lasted some 51 years, why has the government decided to make a new effort in the constitutional field, an effort which was announced in the Speech from the Throne last fall when we indicated the government's intention to introduce in the House a number of initiatives in areas which are of strict federal jurisdiction? The reason, Mr. Speaker, is very simple. 1 suggest that the current situation imposes upon us, the government, who have been elected to represent the people, the obligation to face this issue once again. Of course, several things have changed in Canada during these 51 years, but the rate of acceleration of these changes has been particularly high over the past few years.
We have seen a shift of power relations develop in Canada which has expressed itself in various ways.
One of the ways in which this new relationship has expressed itself is in the increase in the size of all governments. In 1967 expenditures by all governments constituted some 23 per cent of the gross national product; ten years later, in 1977, this had increased to 40 per cent. Even within this increase of 8 per cent it is important to note there had been a shifting of power relationships. While federal spending went up by 3 per cent between 1967 and 1977, provincial and municipal spending together went up by 5 per cent, most of it provincial.
New power relationships were developing. The citizen was faced with governments which were growing in size. Of course the regions were taking on increased importance. The Atlantic regions were surging toward the hope held out to them by the new resource base, particularly the maritime resource. The western provinces had gone from a time when they were small markets, distant markets, and suppliers of raw materials, to the present situation where they comprise some one quarter of the Canadian population. In terms of wealth the three "have" provinces in Canada now comprise in their number two western provinces, Alberta and British Columbia.
And another one coming up fast.

Another one is coming up fast-Saskatchewan. There has obviously been a shift westward in that sense, not only in population but of the centre of economic gravity in Canada.

June 27, 1978
The Constitution
Ontario, of course, has gone increasingly toward a province which is open, hospitable to everyone, and which has shown in the composition of its population that it is multiethnic and very democratic.

Finally, the case of the province of Quebec is well known. For quite some time, constitutional matters were discussed there but, since the month of November 1976, it has become particularly obvious, with the election of a provincial government which set itself the mission of pulling Quebec out of Canada, that the constitution and constitutional matters are of prime importance in that province.
Why, I ask again, should we tackle once again the constitutional problem? Because it is important, Mr. Speaker, that we should try through new documents, through a new constitution, to deal with this new power relationship, the concerns of the citizens, the new requirements of the various areas, and especially, and that may be the absolutely irrefutable reason, of importance to all Canadians and Quebeckers in particular, to prove that new constitutions are a possibility before the citizens of that province have to commit themselves in a referendum on their fate, on their political future.
So, for all those reasons, the government of Canada has decided to come to grips once again with that constitutional matter. Mr. Speaker, efforts were always met with failure on previous occasions because we tried to reach unanimity among the provinces and the federal government, we felt this time that we might solve the problem in two stages, the first of which would entail amending the constitution in such fields as fall within federal jurisdiction, and the second, amending the constitution on matters of joint federal and provincial jurisdictions.
We realize, of course, that it would ill become the federal government to propose amendments regarding provincial jurisdictions without the consent of the provinces. That is why in our determination to solve the constitutional issue, we have decided to take action, and as the bill now before us clearly shows, we have decided to start with the field that comes under our jurisdiction.

It is important to make this point clear, that the Parliament of Canada has, under the present constitution, the power to amend its constitution. Section 91 of the British North America Act in the first paragraph says so quite clearly. When the present constitution, the British North America Act, enumerates the powers of the federal parliament it indicates as the first among those powers the amendment from time to time of the Constitution of Canada in respect of the six areas which are enumerated.
The equivalent of that for the provinces is well known by this House. Section 92 in the first paragraph says that the provinces can amend their constitution from time to time in all
matters except-and then there is one exception, that relating to the office of the lieutenant-governor.
So it is quite clear that the Parliament of Canada can amend the Constitution of Canada except in certain areas which I will return to, and the provinces can amend their constitution except in one area. Indeed, the provinces have repeatedly amended their constitution. Well-known examples of that occurred when a few provinces decided to abolish the legislative council, their second chamber. This was done within very recent times by the province of Quebec. It had been done before by other provinces. It is quite clear that both levels of government can amend their constitution in so far as it concerns matters not excepted under sections 91 and 92, in the first paragraphs. But also it follows that both governments cannot amend the Constitution of Canada acting alone, unilaterally, by mere action of their particular legislature.
We have proposed to the country and to the House of Commons that we exercise our rights under section 91, and that we amend the Constitution of Canada in several areas which I will detail briefly, but none of them, of course, are areas which are covered or concerned by the exceptions, namely, section 91 first paragraph. Before going into details on that, let me add a word about patriation and amending formulas.

From a jurisdictional point of view, where does the problem of repatriating the constitution and finding an amendment formula belong constitutionally? It could be either in the first or in the second phase, depending on our discussions with the provinces. In fact, the patriation could very well take place in the first phase since it would in no way affect the distribution of powers among the federal government and the provincial governments. At the same time, if we patriate the constitution and agree on an amending formula, the participation of the provinces would be required some way or other. That is why the provinces might prefer to postpone until the second phase the discussion on patriation and the amending formula. For our part, Mr. Speaker, we are proposing a bill dealing with our powers and jurisdiction. That does not mean that we are not prepared or even not anxious to discuss that second phase when the provinces will want to do so but we know that should not be done without the agreement of the provinces to open the discussion.
I know we have been blamed for starting with what is not more important. That is a point of view, Mr. Speaker. Of course, the sharing of powers is extremely important but I also remind the House that we are dealing in the province of Quebec with a government which does not want to discuss any sharing of powers but rather the handing over of the totality of political powers to the province of Quebec. Of course, that is a situation we cannot consider. I know that the other provinces cannot entertain it either. So it would be useless to say: let us


June 27, 1978

start the discussion there when we know that at least one of the participants refuses to support that discussion. So I believe we have not only the right but a near obligation to move ahead on that constitutional issue and move ahead in the area where we have the right to move ahead. It could be that in previous discussions the constitutional issue concerned mainly the experts-lawyers, politicians, academics and news commentators. But I believe I am right, Mr. Speaker, in saying that this time the constitutional issue concerns everyone. It concerns Canadians, particularly those in Quebec who are looking at their future, their political destiny with a measure of anguish, and it concerns that very large number of people who wanted to show their interest in the constitutional issue before the Pepin-Robarts commission or other forums.
So we made that proposal, and to try to explain it without going into the technical details, I would like to say that we think that three major problems stand in the way of harmony and unity in this country. The first one has to do with the relationships of the people with governments. The second is the language problem, the fact that we have two official languages. The third one has to do with regionalism, namely a certain alineation of the regions vis-a-vis the government and the central parliament.

I would like to show how this constitution bill attempts to deal with these three very important sources of uncertainty and division in Canada.
Let us begin with what I suppose could be described as the alienation of the citizen toward governments, big governments, as I indicated earlier. They have been getting bigger as modern governments in industrial societies feel they must deal with an increasing number of areas. At the same time as the citizen has been asking his governments to do more things for him, he has been subjected to legislation which naturally reduces the area of his liberties. For that he has been asking certain guarantees against big governments.
At the same time citizens in Canada seeing this evolving power of relationship, sensing frustration toward big governments, federal, provincial, and sometimes even municipal levels, sensing the divisions between regions and the central government which often express themselves in federal-provincial tensions, sensing too the linguistic problem which has caused a great deal of puzzlement and sometimes annoyance among citizens where minorities, French minorities in other provinces or English-speaking minorities in Quebec, also with the increasing number of Canadians of other ethnic stock than that of the French or those from the British Isles who have wanted to know their place in this society, have wanted to know the constitutional rank that was given them as well as the rank that the native peoples were concerned about. We attempted to deal with all of these problems in the following ways.
First of all the preamble, the statement of aims, which I will not recite here, does try to create for Canadians a sense of purpose, a sense of identity. It does try to tell them in
The Constitution
reasonably simple and intelligible language that in Canada we honour and respect diversity, but that basically we are all united and we all share the same goals, goals of equality of opportunity from any part of this country where one may come, or from whatever part of the world one may emigrate to Canada. We tend to express this in the preamble and in the statement of aims in a way in which Canadians can feel that their government in a constitution binds itself to recognize these basic rights, freedoms, and the right to seek one's fulfilment in equality of opportunity.
The next problem with which we have to deal is the problem of regional alienation. The expression is well known and often used. Essentially, it comes and is expressed from and by the people who feel that they in some way belong to regions which are either too distant from Ottawa in terms of geography, political representation, economic fulfilment, or linguistic equality.
These various feelings of alienation have been the object of concern by all governments. That is why so many of them have been talking about constitutional problems and why so many other groups have been talking about constitutional problems. The official opposition recently published a paper, a white paper or policy paper, on the constitution. There is a group called, 1 believe, Canada West, which has published such a paper. There is a group of academics from Toronto. The government of Ontario has published policy papers trying to deal with this problem.
Looking at all these documents, it appears there are two ways essentially of approaching this problem of regional alienation. The first would be for the constitution to transfer vastly increased powers to the regions so that in the regions or in the provinces those powers would be exercised by governments which are at least closer geographically to the centres of population.
This approach of massive decentralization, which takes various forms, is one which this government rejects. We believe that whatever form the constitution takes, there must always be a central government able to speak for all Canadians in all parts of Canada in areas which are important in the lives of those people.
Hear, hear!

We think it would be a mistake to try to save the unity of Canada merely by saving its geographical entity. We think that unless the central government can indeed govern effectively over all citizens in the country, we might have saved the map of Canada but we would not have saved the reality of a nation, a people united in their purposes and seeking to fulfil their destiny together.
That is why, along with massive decentralization, we reject other approaches which tend in the same direction. 1 would name solutions such as associate statehood or loose confederations as other forms of constitutional change which would tend to save the country by destroying it in the long run.

June 27, 1978
The Constitution
Therefore, if we cannot and should not solve the problem of regional alienation by giving powers out to the regions, we look at the other approach and feel that that must consist in bringing, in some way, the regions to the centre, making sure that that feeling of alienation which exists in the regions is in some way healed by making the regions feel that they are truly represented in some ways at the centre.
There are various ways of doing that, Mr. Speaker. One, of course, would be through changing the approach in this very chamber. We could, for example, decide that in the future the electoral system in this country for election to the Elouse of Commons would be one based on proportion representation. In this way the citizens of the regions would find that their national government would tend to be formed of coalitions, of groups, of parties speaking for the regions, since this indeed would be the object.
This is a remedy which has been examined by some and, I am sure, will be debated by others. However, it is an approach that this government also rejected for a very simple reason. We fear not so much governments of coalition, although it is certainly very debatable whether that is a very desirable approach, but governments of coalition which would be based on rivalries between regions rather than slight ideological or party differences. To our mind, that would not unite the country, but divide it further. This House, parliament, would become a place where regions would quarrel amongst themselves and seek alliances, not to further the national good of all the country but in order to further their own particular regional or provincial interests.
That is why we have rejected that approach and chosen instead to try to reform our constitution by acting in a way which is common to most federal systems, acting through the second chamber and seeking ways in which that second chamber, which we call in this bill the House of the Federation, can in some way bring the concerns and the debates from the regions to the centre. They can make sure that whatever concerns are expressed and felt in the various regions of Canada will be debated and resolved not only and not mainly at the provincial level, but here on Parliament Hill in the parliament of all Canadians. For that we have decided to produce certain modifications to the second chamber, the House of the Federation.
Here again various approaches would have been possible. One would be to have the members of the second chamber elected directly by the people. As everyone knows, this is the system which is in practice in the United States and in Australia, where the senators are elected directly by the people, according to certain percentages and numbers across the totality of the federation. In this way the upper house, the second chamber, reflects not national parties which are geared and oriented toward the expression of the greatest common good of the whole country, but is filled with people who are elected to speak more precisely for their regions.

This, once again, is a solution which will be debated and on which the government is anxious to hear argument. But we rejected this for a very simple reason, too. It is that experience has shown in Australia-and, I think, theory would also demonstrate-that this system of direct election of two chambers, the House of Commons and the House of the Federation, would result almost inevitably in difficulties in the functioning of the parliamentary system. There would be the question to which of the houses is the government responsible, and what should be done in the case of an irreconcilable difference between the two chambers? What would be the result at a time of double dissolution, and so on?
It is because of such questions that we are afraid the introduction of this system is not compatible with the parliamentary method of government and would tend to lean more toward the presidential system where somebody above the elected chambers, someone responsible to the whole country- a president of sorts-would exercise legislative authority. That is the difficulty to which direct representation in the second chamber would lead us. I submit this would also be the difficulty if we had one chamber, elected by PR, which was the forum of contending regionalist parties. We would inevitably drift, I submit, toward a presidential system since some authority above these quarrelling regions would have to be elected, such authority coming directly from the people. Therefore, through a process of elimination, Mr. Speaker, we ended up with a second chamber which would not be elected but which would be appointed.
Now it may be asked: why not have the provinces appoint the members of the second chamber in a system which would be somewhat attuned to the system of the government in the Federal Republic of Germany? Our view is that the provinces have a function within the constitution which is to exercise the jurisdiction contained in the constitution, and particularly in section 92, or some modification thereof, with authority over the citizens of those respective provinces in areas of provincial jurisdiction. We do not think it would be the right approach to tell the provinces, whose authority is absolute within their spheres of government in the provinces, to determine also how the national government shall be managed and how the national parliament shall be run.
We think it is important for the people of the regions to know that they, as regions, have spokesmen in the second chamber. That is why we have proposed that members of the House of the Federation be chosen by a system which ensures that the result will correspond to the popular vote in those different provinces-not a system which corresponds to the will of the national government or of the provincial governments, but a system which equates itself to the voting pattern of the people of the provinces voting sometimes in provincial elections and sometimes in federal elections. This is the result which is proposed to the House in this constitutional amendment bill, Mr. Speaker.
It is said it will be very complicated. I suppose it is possible to look for alternative ways, and I repeat the government is
June 27, 1978

anxious to hear discussion on all these questions. But I submit that every constitutional change is probably met with the fear that it will be too complicated. Certainly the system which exists in connection with the Senate in the United States, with a third being elected every two years for six years, and the congressional system, must have seemed very complex when the constitution of the United States of America was brought forward. The system of the Bonn government must also have seemed very complicated when it was introduced.
In fairness, Mr. Speaker, I ask those Canadians who want to debate constitutional problems and look for solutions, to consider this whole matter, going back to the first principles I have put before the House-how do we bring the regions to the centre and make sure that in some way we end the feeling of alienation which eventually, if left to develop, will destroy the legitimacy of the national parliament? How can these questions be resolved in a constitution?
Finally, I said there was a third area where problems in Canada were acute and had to find their solution in the constitutional bill. That is the area of language. I believe it is the matter which is of most concern to the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) who just crossed the floor.
I believe it must be for that reason, because 1 know that when the hon. gentleman was a member of cabinet he was most earnest and ardent in his search for greater equity for the regions. I doubt whether he could object to any honest effort to ensure greater representation for the regions. If, as I suspect, he crossed the floor because of a disagreement on the question of language, I can only say that I respect his decision but do not deny that it is a profound disagreement and one which could not be reconciled.
We on this side of the House take it as a basic tenet of Canada that we must avoid any constitutional or legal development which would result in one province speaking only or mainly French, and all the other provinces speaking only English.
Hear, hear!

Given the historic and demographic data of this country, I think it is folly to say that bilingualism is divisive. Again, given the historic and demographic data, 1 think one must conclude that equality of the two official languages is not divisive but the only way in which this country will remain united.
Hear, hear!

1 say this because it is the only way in which English-speaking Canadians will continue to live and want to live in Quebec and feel at home and equal citizens there, and because it is the only way in which French-speaking Canadians will continue and want to continue living in other parts of Canada. And it is the only way whereby we can avoid developing in Canada two nations, one French-speaking in Quebec and the other English-speaking elsewhere, which would inevitably lead to the dissolution of this country either into the form
The Constitution
of a loose confederation of associated states or of two nations expressed as sovereign independent states.
The only way in which this problem will be solved will be to tackle honestly and squarely the problem of the French and English languages. Here again, this is what is attempted in this bill. It is attempted, first, at the federal level by the linguistic guarantees which are part of the bill of rights. As I wanted to indicate earlier, the bill of rights covers a multitude of areas- pc'itical, democratic, civil and, of course, anti-discrimination provisions-but it also covers linguistic provisions and ensures that at the federal level the spirit of the Official Languages Act, which was adopted by all parties in this House, is incorporated into this constitution. It also ensures that the provisions of section 133 of the present BNA Act are incorporated in this constitution, putting both languages on an equal footing, not only in parliament and in the records and publications of parliament but also in the courts.
Insofar as provincial jurisdictions are concerned we can only suggest ways in which the provinces will assure this linguistic equality, and the way in which we approach it, of course, is to impose-to suggest that three provinces accept for themselves the provisions which Quebec has as regards its minority under section 133. We know that section 133 of the present constitution gives certain fundamental guarantees to the Englishspeaking people of that province.
We think it would be unrealistic and probably impossible, within the future which I can foresee, to see the provisions of Section 133 which protect the English in Quebec apply in every province of Canada, but we do suggest that the provisions should protect French-speaking Canadians in Canada in those three provinces where 95 per cent of all Francophone Canadians live, that is to say, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario. We realize that we will cause some difficulties but probably not that much greater than have been caused in Quebec for the past 111 years. However, once again this is in an area of provincial jurisdiction. We are seeking solutions here, and we are asking for provincial contributions in this area.
As far as education is concerned, we do not differentiate. The approach of this constitution is to protect official language minorities in the area of education wherever they exist, the English-speaking minority in Quebec and the French-speaking minority in every other province. We think this is the proper solution.
I know that some provinces will say that we should not be discussing education because it is purely provincial, but the way in which this constitution is couched will permit the provinces to see that indeed we are not attempting here to legislate in that area. We are suggesting the way in which we think the linguistic problem at the provincial level will be solved, but I merely want to remind those who make that point that we have in our present constitution, and have had since 1867, provision for the federal government to intervene in areas of legislation and to protect minorities in the educational system. Therefore, the concept is not new.

June 27, 1978
The Constitution
It is true that when the Fathers of Confederation approached this problem 111 years ago they defined minorities then in religious terms because there was a certain equation between religious and linguistic problems in the province of Quebec and, indeed, at that time in the province of Manitoba, but the concept of the federal government's protecting minorities in the area of education is not a new one. It is 111 years old, and all I want to say is that we are not proposing the continuance of this protection by the federal government; we are suggesting that all governments in a sense give up some of their jurisdiction, not to other levels of government but to the citizen in a declaration of rights, including that of linguistic rights.

Mr. Speaker, that is about all I had to say on the bill now under consideration and 1 chose not to get into technicalities because I hope the debate will bear on basic issues rather than matters of detail. Indeed that is why we are not on second reading of this bill today. Instead we are discussing a motion to establish a committee of the House of Commons and the Senate to study the bill and other constitutional documents which may be referred to it by the government or which the committee itself may wish to study. I am thinking particularly of the proposal concerning constitutional matters made by the Progressive Conservative party one or two months ago if my memory serves me well.
So it is important to remember that this bill, which, as I have been trying to explain over the last thirty minutes or so, embodies the solutions proposed at this stage by the government and the Liberal Party of Canada, has not gone beyond first reading yet. In other words, before its re-introduction in the next session, there will be not only, I hope, a very positive discussion in the joint committee of both Houses, but also possibly a report from the Pepin-Robarts commission which we might take into account in drafting the bill for the next session and that there will be discussions at the provincial level. In fact, my colleagues, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde) and other ministers have already met the premiers to explain the spirit, the philosophy and the economy of the bill and we are at their disposal to provide them with further explanations.
Mr. Speaker, we know that there will be a meeting of premiers in August and that one of the issues on the agenda will be those constitutional proposals. So I repeat, it should be well understood that it is not a definitive or unilateral action that precludes any discussion. It is the result of the ideas developed by the government with the support of the Liberal caucus. It is the result of our thinking but, as I said, we are prepared to continue the debate and improve the way in which we shall be able to study the bill.
I note, Mr. Speaker, that I have forgotten a very small item in my outline. I would like to refer to it simply to show the House that we believe this to be important. When I suggested

that the regions should be represented within the legislative body in the second chamber, I should have added that we also want the provinces to feel represented, or in any case not alienated, with regard to the national government and the supreme court, and certain proposals to this effect are contained in the bill.
But it is time that I concluded, Mr. Speaker. In closing, I would simply like to say once again that we do not believe that a constitutional bill can lead the country towards greater harmony or unity if the bill is not debated and eventually accepted by the great majority of Canadians. This is why we have proceeded in this way by moving a motion to establish a committee. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this committee can report to us in the coming months. As for me, I am convinced that we owe it to ourselves and that we owe it to Canadians to give them finally a constitution written, passed, proclaimed in Canada, for Canadians, by Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, naturally I am pleased that the government has decided to establish a parliamentary committee to look at the question of constitutional reform. I should say to my hon. friends to the left that we are pleased this is a joint committee, and that we intend to do our part to keep it that way. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated, and as the House will recall, this is something we proposed more than a year ago. Frankly I think it would have been even more effective than today to have had a parliamentary committee representing the whole of the country and dealing with the matter. At that time, it was turned down by the government.
I have one or two comments in direct response to what was said by the Prime Minister. I want to raise these matters at the beginning, because they reflect some attitudes of mind of his which may well be causing difficulty in the country. He may well disagree with the suggestion that those attitudes of his causes problems, but probably it is good for him to know that we on this side of the House think they do.
He made reference to the very real difficulty, and I think he used the word "impossibility", of dealing with one province which has elected a government that is determined to separate the country, the province of Quebec. Perhaps it will be impossible for any federal government to deal with that province. However, it is important for the country and the House to recognize that virtually nothing has been proposed to that government, or indeed the other provincial governments of confederation, by the federal government which might indicate some willingness on the part of Ottawa to consider very seriously some of the substantive jurisdictional changes of power that will be essential, if we are going to have a system which is satisfactory.
I regret the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) is not in the House. Indeed, in those relatively isolated cases when something has been tried by the government, as was attempted in relation to the immigration arrangement, an agreement was reached between the Government of Canada and the province of Quebec.
June 27, 1978

From time to time, even in the absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), the fact that everyone in the House of Commons is a federalist needs to be underlined. Everyone wants to see elected in the province of Quebec a government which is committed to maintaining the Canadian federal system. There is no disagreement about that. It seems that one route to that goal will be to demonstrate that there can be changes in a system which a large number of Quebeckers and a large number of other Canadians believe is not working. Frankly they are not particularly interested in patriation formulae or amending formulae. They are interested in the effectiveness with which governments do their jobs.
It would be very helpful to making a case for federalism if there were a much greater determination on the part of this federal government to sit down with the provinces, including Quebec, in an attempt to reach a specific agreement on specific changes of power where a failure to agree now means that services are not being well delivered. It means frustration is high not just with government, but potentially with the system.
I do not want to go on at any length, but I hope the Prime Minister's view of Quebec, that it is absolutely impossible to deal with that government, even though his colleagues have found that it is possible to deal with them on matters such as the immigration question, will not be used as an excuse to stop him from sitting down with the other premiers of Canada, including the premier of Quebec if he will come, to discuss specific changes which may make modern the Canadian federal system.
I could not help but be amused when I heard the Prime Minister speaking about the problems of Canadian citizens dealing within a larger society with distant governments and more complex matters, and the fact that he went back to his quite long standing concern for a charter of rights. It is agreed that a charter of rights would be of very real value. Certainly the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) took an important initiative in introducing the Bill of Rights. It is quite important for us to make the point that the introduction of a freedom of information law in this country, or the determination of a willingness to amend the Official Secrets Act, would at least be as effective as a charter by demonstrating in practice what we proclaim in a charter as regards human rights.
Hear, hear!

In case it is not clear, the point of that is: I think the Government of Canada should realize that there are ways to demonstrate good will and that there are ways to make progress, other than by drafting laws and proclamations. They and we will be judged very much by our actions, as well as by our declarations.
As I said at the outset, we look forward to the establishment of this parliamentary committee. Certainly we will do our part as the official opposition to ensure that there is a thorough and
The Constitution
informed consideration of the contents of the document tabled by the Prime Minister. I think it is important to make it clear now in the House of Commons that we believe it would be wrong to attempt to have parliamentary consideration of constitutional changes limited by or to this document. We think it would be wrong to let the government pretend that presentation of this so-called bill exhausts the obligations of the federal government regarding constitutional reform.
[ Translation]
If you would allow me, Mr. Speaker, I would like to clarify those two statements. First of all, the exact status of this proposal is not clear. It has been presented in the form of a bill, which implies that the basic proposal of the government has already been established and that only the details can be changed. However, the proposal is referred to the committee without trying to obtain an agreement in principle on the part of the government, which leads us to believe that the government considers that it is not really a definitive proposal. I hope the second interpretation is the right one. We certainly intend to consider this bill as a white paper-as a simple proposal- and we hope that the government will not try to restrict the debate to the limited scope covered by its own proposal.
Indeed what partly differentiates a constitution from other laws is the fact that if it is to apply to the whole community a constitution must so reflect it. The Parliament of Canada is the best representative of the whole nation. This is why, as I have stated, my party proposed a year ago the creation of a parliamentary committee but I suggest that the committee will have to wonder whether it is in itself representative enough so that a sufficient number of Canadians who favour federalism as a form of government be able to consider this Parliament as a legitimate source for a new federal constitution.

I suggest we have at least two deficiencies. One has to do with our nature. In constitutional questions we represent only the national part of the Canadian partnership. The provinces are not here. The other limitation, which is quite a serious one, has to do with the mandate of this parliament. In normal circumstances this parliament would be ended, and the people of Canada would be choosing a fresh parliament and a new government. There is real doubt as to whether a parliament, which hangs on beyond its normal life, has the mandate to propose changes so fundamental as constitutional reform. Certainly any claim to legitimacy we have would be weakened seriously if we consider proposals from only one source.
As the Prime Minister indicated, it is our good fortune that a number of responsible Canadian organizations and individuals proposed constitutional reforms well before the government document was tabled. My list is not at all complete, but I think of groups like the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Advisory Council on Confederation, the government of the province of British Columbia, the premiers of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and New Brunswick, at least; the C.D. Howe Research Institute, the Canada West Foundation and, as the

June 27, 1978
The Constitution
Prime Minister mentioned, my own party. We are pleased to be joined in June of 1978 by the proposals of the Government of Canada.
I would hope that some of those recommendations from the groups 1 have enumerated would be considered by the committee, and considered with some care and in some detail. Naturally, I think it would be a terrible waste of the money of the taxpayers of Canada, and an insult to the members of that commission, if we were not able to consider in the committee the recommendations, however tentative at this stage, of the Pepin-Robarts royal commission.
This is not an idle observation. Canadians have lived long enough with this government to distrust both its motives and its judgment on questions of constitutional reform. Many of us are puzzled-I tried to find a good neutral word and I think "puzzled" probably serves-by the change in tactics and by the timetable this government has adopted since it decided not to call a federal general election.
A year ago parliament was deliberately denied a voice in constitutional reform. Today we have what appears to be a bill going to a committee. Six weeks ago, as the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) mentioned, not long ago, in explaining his decision not to call an election, the Prime Minister spoke of the urgent economic initiatives his government still had to take. Parliament adjourns in four days and no new economic measure has been proposed. But what we do have is a deadline for concluding a very complex constitutional debate.
These inconsistencies inevitably increase suspicion that the government is using constitutional reform for partisan purposes, and that suspicion is going to be much greater if the government seeks to rush the work of this committee, seeks to stampede it through, or if it seeks to limit unduly the questions the committee can consider.
[ Translation]
At the beginning I stated that the government cannot claim that its obligations in the field of constitutional reform are limited to issuing a document and setting a deadline. Indeed, the job of the federal government has only begun. This document deals mainly with its form. The true disagreements in Canada deal with the basic issue which is how to share power in a great diversified federal country. The present document does not even touch this issue.
Yet this is an issue which is the cornerstone of the problem. In fact a witty person could even conclude that one of the purposes of that proposal-with its proportional representation, its consultation process regarding judges, its council of state-is to divert attention so that people forget the urgent need of starting to reach an agreement regarding the powers which will be exercised by the various levels of government in a mordern and reformed type of federalism.

Sir, I have heard and read transcripts of the Prime Minister's remarks before-his lamentation, really-about his ten years of failure on constitutional reform. It is true that the initiatives that were begun by Mr. Fulton and Mr. Favreau have lost considerable momentum in the last ten years. As the late Prime Minister Pearson said, "The process has, of course, continued, although in the years since I retired it has lost much of its impetus. I regret that very much."
1 think it is important for this House of Commons and for the people of Canada, as we embark on this latest step in constitutional consideration, that we put that failure in some kind of perspective. What have failed have been formulae, a formula to amend and a formula to repatriate. What has not failed, but what very sadly has not been tried enough, is agreement on specific changes in the conduct or jurisdiction of different levels of government.
There have been some successes, including some by this government. I mentioned earlier a very real success in the field of immigration. There may well be some others that I do not know of, although I would be surprised if this government had any successes that it had failed to communicate at substantial public expense. These successes are exceptions, because for the last ten years constitutional reform has been viewed by this government as a legal question, not a political question.
Earlier Canadian governments-governments that were less preoccupied with legal form-were far more successful in getting political agreements, ranging from the winter works program, the equalization grants, and the Fleming-Sauve formula, initiated during the years when the right hon. member for Prince Albert was prime minister, and then through the Canada Pension Plan and Medicare with Mr. Pearson. Both those governments gave significant attention to the constitution as a legal document, but they were also able to look beyond legal reform; their eyes were not limited to the horizon of legal reform, and they were able to make the constitution work with an agreement among partners in this country.
That brings me in these remarks to probably the single most serious danger in this document. It is a danger about which I am pleased to note the Prime Minister was a little defensive in his own remarks. It is the attempt, however disguised, to have Ottawa unilaterally amend the partnership that is confederation.
The government argues with energetic innocence that it confines itself to its own strict jurisdiction, and does nothing that has any influence on a province. That, unfortunately, is not true. Anyone could go on at great length about this, but let me deal just for a moment with the supreme court.
At an earlier time unilateral federal amendment in respect of the supreme court was not considered by the provinces to be a serious matter, and hence it was not included originally in exceptions for federal amendment. That was at a time when the supreme court was not the final court of appeal. It is now the final court of appeal, and surely provinces have to be consulted as to a change of this magnitude which the govern-

June 27, 1978

ment is proposing, and there is not provision in this House at this stage for that kind of consultation.
There are other instances of that kind of difficulty. Proposed section 14(2) in this bill, and since I think none of us is sure exactly what stage of this bill we have reached I hope you will allow me to quote from some of the specific provisions, sir, states:
Any individual has the right to use English or French, as he or she may choose, in any of the debates or other proceedings of the legislative assembly of any province.
Proposed section 16(2) says:
Either English or French may be used by any person in, or in any pleading or process in or issuing from, any court of Ontario, Quebec or New Brunswick.
Those are the provinces to which the Prime Minister is making the suggestion, and unfortunately he slipped and called it the "imposition", which is probably a closer reflection of his state of mind.
Proposed section 19(2), and this is a rather long quotation, states:
Any member of the public in any province has the right to use English or French, as he or she may choose, in communicating with any principal office of a department or agency of the executive government of that province, or of a judicial, quasi-judicial or administrative body or Crown corporation established by or pursuant to a law of that province, where that office is located within an area of that province in which it is determined, in such manner as may be prescribed or authorized by the legislature of that province, that a substantial number of persons within the population use that language.
I recognize that the Prime Minister has already begun the argument, and some of his colleagues will carry it, that these provisions will not apply in a province unless the province agrees. The point I want to emphasize is that we have no business, in this House of Commons, passing a declaration expressing a direction as to how a province should act within the exclusive jurisdiction of that province prior to the province establishing its own considered opinion.
I have read the explanation. 1 know that the official explanation is to have federal parliamentary approval granted in advance so that there can be a very quick indication of federal approval and a very quick closing of the arrangement once the provinces agree. That may be the excuse, but the much more likely result would be to attempt to have that action by parliament give legitimacy to an action the legislature may consider to be impractical or impossible. It amounts to an official statement of direction in a field that is beyond our jurisdiction and beyond our competence.
Although proposed section 17 may provide some protection in this matter, a fair reading of section 16(2), which I quoted earlier, would require every traffic ticket in Ontario to be capable of being argued in either official language. In many parts of the real world that will be impossible for a long time to come, and parliament should not attempt to pressure any province into enacting what it cannot honour.
