[ Translation]
This approach involves two dangers, one specific, the other global. The specific danger concerns language rights and, more particularly, the objective of creating a climate in which residents and governments of predominantly English-speaking provinces choose to significantly increase services and encourage communication in French. In certain circumstances, it is useful to recognize rights and pass legislation. That is the conclusion arrived at by New Brunswick. In other cases, it may be preferable to go ahead without official declarations or provincial laws. As hon. members of the House know, I gave full support to the Official Languages Act and my predecessor, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), did more than any other member of the House to gain acceptance for this act throughout Canada, especially in the west.
This federal act is now part of the basic principles of our system and in trying to make it accepted we have learned a few things. We have learned that most people prefer to have a choice rather than be forced into something. It is encouraging to see the important practical progress made towards offering bilingual services in most English-speaking provinces. The progress made in Ontario is well known. It may not be so well known, however, that in my own province, Alberta, the number of students at the primary and secondary levels who learn French is increasing constantly. It rose from 6,323 students in 18 school boards last year to 7,601 students in 20 school boards this year.
This is happening at a time when the total number of students in Alberta is decreasing, but also when registration at the university college of Saint-Jean, in Edmonton, has increased substantially, especially among students who intend to teach French in Alberta. I can truthfully say, as one who knows that Albertans would rather choose than submit to restraints, that the passing of a piece of legislation may perhaps delay progress.
In my view, which, I think, was also the view of my predecessor, a personal type of leadership is more efficient than the mere passing of legislation.

That, sir, is the specific danger to which I refer.
The general danger is that the provinces, like the rest of us, do not much like the idea of being pushed around. One of the major sources of conflict in our country in the last ten years is that the federal government has tried so often to push provinces around, and there is every danger that the device of having parliament pronounce on matters within provincial jurisdiction, and pronounce before the provinces do, will be seen as one more cause of discord. There is already evidence to that effect from a variety of premiers representing a variety of political parties.
I think this is particularly true because in the course of the last six weeks we seem to have revived around here that atmosphere of confrontation between Ottawa and the provinces, from which we were happily freed for a long time. I

June 27, 1978
The Constitution
remember that the Prime Minister actually called the premiers to go on television with him during one break in the pattern of his conduct of federal-provincial relations. But we seem to be back again at that attitude of Ottawa going out and picking fights with the provinces. We saw it clearly in the very stubborn manner in which the federal government proceeded with the invasion of provincial jurisdiction on the sales tax issue. We saw it again in the declarations of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), and we certainly see it in the lottery question. Indeed, we have a hint of that in the repeated assertions of the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde), that he is not going to let the objections of mere provinces stop his amending the common constitution.
We have a document here, sir, with a handful of specific proposals. They are going to be considered in detail at committee along with, as 1 have said, and I hope, a lot of other relevant proposals. Some of these provisions are curious, to say the least. 1 find it bizarre, for example, for the federal government to propose to the provinces that it is going to suspend the power of disallowance in regard to a province, which everybody knows is a useless power, when the provinces have agreed to certain federal conditions. The Prime Minister is the worldly expert in the House on forums and constitutions, but it seems to me to be odd that a constitution should enshrine the practice of offering a treat to those who are good. It is no wonder that this government is called paternalistic, with an attitude like that.
1 also think that this government does not know much about the psychology of the people responding to treaties. There may be some kids around who may be cajoled by the offer of ice cream, but I do not think there would be very many who would respond to an empty cone, which is what we have here in regard to the power of disallowance.
Another curiosity is that the document extends constitutional status to the office of Prime Minister of Canada but not, so far as I can see, to the office of premier of a province. Again, it proposes an extraordinary safeguard, the double majority vote, and it accords that-and this is quite important-in relation to linguistic rights, but not in relation to provincial rights.
The Prime Minister spoke at some length about the role of the provinces, the role of the regions in making national decisions. As he knows, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) on behalf of my party put forward for discussion a proposal for Senate reform, a proposal which we have found was contentious enough in itself, which clearly established the second chamber as an institution that would allow the provinces to participate directly in national decisions. This proposal the Prime Minister has made, as he has been gracious enough to admit, is very different. What he proposes, when you strip everything away, is representation of party interests, not of provincial interests.
Indeed, when you read through the document, proposed section 64(1) prohibits membership in the upper chamber of any elected member of a legislature or of the House of Commons. However, proposed section 60 allows a member of
the federal cabinet, but not a member of a provincial cabinet, to be invited to participate in questioning or debate in that second chamber. These matters are contentious in detail and in concept. They require the most thorough consideration and debate, and that is why my colleagues and I hope very seriously there will be no attempt to rush this matter through or to limit the agenda of the committee.
The Prime Minister, when he began, looked back to Mackenzie King and spoke of the historic concept and the history of constitutional change in this country. I think we all recognize, sir, that history, including history in a country like Canada, is made a step at a time. It may very well be that we are at such a step now. It may very well be that that is involved in this document or, more likely, that it will emerge from some of the considerations of the parliamentary committee.
1 would like to repeat that it is the determination of members of my party to pursue serious proposals seriously. I think it is important that we recognize, too, that constitutional problems in a country will never be resolved, because there are always going to be differences among the people who make up a country and among the regions which make up a country. We may very well be able to change some of the institutions that are here. We may very well have to bring the actual document home, but it is important to recognize that any political system, particularly a large federal system, will always be defining itself and always be re-arranging itself. 1 should like to risk conventional wisdom by saying that, in my view, we have done that relatively well through much of our history as a country.
We face some particular challenges now, some of them very serious. One is a failure to nurture in the province of Quebec paticularly, a sense of security regarding the Quebecois culture and regarding its capacity to survive as a federal state.
Another challenge, as the Prime Minister admitted in his analysis but did not appear to recognize in his response, is the failure to respond to the new potential of our various regions, particularly of our distant regions, a potential brought by the discovery and development of our resources, by a movement of population, and by the simple fact that some of them now have power to exercise. It is a challenge that has been effected in no small measure. I will not go into this at more length at this time. I have done so on other occasions and I shall do so again. It is a problem that has been caused in no small measure by an unusually centralist government that has, throughout its life in office, reached out to try to gather to itself powers that would be more effectively exercised by municipal governments, by provinces, by the private sector, and by voluntary agencies. That has added appreciably to the tensions that we have to resolve and relieve in this country.
It is essential that we are able to find in this parliament- and I have full confidence that the committee that is established will help us in that search-responses that recognize the failures I have indicated, and that establish structures and attitudes that will serve the future of this country.

June 27, 1978

1 very much hope that this document which is before us, and the discussion to which it gives rise, will prove to be valuable. 1 must say that I have more confidence in the usefulness of the discussion than I do in the usefulness of the document. The committee must have something to start with, however, and I am pleased that we have this document at last.
Whatever comes out of the discussion of structures, whatever we happen to do to the other place, what is absolutely essential is that we restore in this country a sense of partnership and co-operation among governments. That just does not exist now, although it is clear that it can exist if governments want to make it exist.
I will not elaborate on the experience I had as leader of this party in drawing together the premiers from four very different provinces at Kingston almost a year ago to get agreement on specific changes. We were able to get it not because we came from one party but because we came with one common purpose, which was to come to agree and not to come to disagree. I recommend that experience to the Prime Minister for the length of time he has left to exercise it.
The point is that in the provinces of Canada there is clearly a willingness to sit down and try to make some of the changes in particular powers, and in the administration of particular powers, that can make our federal system function far more effectively. That will is there among the provinces. The very real question, far more important than the contents of this bill, far more important 1 regret to say than the work of the committee we are establishing, the fundamental, important thing we have to do is to get the federal government to recognize again that it is part of a partnership and it is going to have to deal with the other partners in confederation on that basis. If that can be done I think we have the best possible prospect for success as a nation.
I can give the assurance to the Prime Minister on behalf of those members of my party who will be serving on that committee, that they will carry out their responsibilities in a very thorough and serious way. I say to him, since he is for a while longer Prime Minister of the country, that I hope he will change some of the attitudes that have caused so many of the problems in this country in the last ten years. I hope he will recognize that we can get agreement of some specific changes of jurisdiction, and that we can get agreement on making the federal system work if there is the same will at the federal level that has been demonstrated in so many cases at the provincial level.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in the opening sentence of the explanatory document for the bill we are discussing today regarding the process of referring it to a committee, the following is written to describe the purpose of the bill:
-to promote the cohesion and well-being of our federation and all its parts.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke this afternoon he essentially made the same point in justifying and
The Constitution
setting the framework for the legislation we are examining in general terms today. He said its central concern was threefold in nature. It was to deal with the place that Canadians would find themselves in as individuals within our confederation; second, it was aimed at dealing with regional alienation, and third were linguistic rights, an important concern throughout the history of our country.
The purpose of the bill is very broad, and as the Prime Minister indicated in his tone, and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in his, it is very serious. This means that in assessing the bill we must do so in that very broad, historic context. We must ask if it comes to grips with the serious question of national unity which has plagued our country for months, indeed, for years.
In assessing it we must all keep two things in mind, particularly we members of parliament who tend to be preoccupied with laws and regulations and who must face both questions. The first is whether, as a constitutional document, it is adequate in terms of providing a legal framework for nationhood. Does it adequately provide a new constitutional framework for over 20 million highly divergent Canadians representing many cultures, but with two principal cultures and two official languages? Does it meet the real needs of economically divergent parts of the country populated in different degrees of concentration? It seems to me that is a fundamental question that has to be answered in a positive way if we are going to say this package of proposals is the kind that, as a parliament, we should recommend be accepted by the people of Canada and the provinces.
Second-and I think it is very important that we deal with this second question-quite apart from its adequacies as a constitutional document we have to ask whether the issues, the tensions, the problems, the concerns about regional inequality, the concerns about language rights, can be resolved by any constitutional approach. That seems to me to be a pretty fundamental question in itself. If the answer is no, then as politicians at this point in our history we have a pretty basic obligation to provide some alternative answers than that which will be provided by a good, bad, or indifferent set of constitutional proposals.
1 want to deal with the first question this afternoon, and to do so not by assessing all of the bill's proposals but by commenting on those which seem to me to be most essential to our concerns as a people at this time. During the summer the committee, comprised of members from all parts of the House, will be considering in detail the whole range of specifics to be found in the bill. My purpose this afternoon is much more restricted.
First of all I want to say very categorically what I find, and what my colleagues find, to be very acceptable and very good in the bill. First, like all Canadians, we find it desirable at long last to have our own written constitution here in Canada instead of in some distant part of the world.

June 27, 1978
The Constitution
Second, we think the proposal that the provinces have some say in the selection of judges in the Supreme Court is a good one.
Third, the proposal we have embedded in the constitution, that of a charter of basic rights, and fundamental liberty, including linguistic rights, we also think is a good proposal. However, we think there are problems associated with the implementation of this particular proposal, but the essential principle we accept and we commend the government for introducing it.
Finally, among those items found in the bill which are desirable and good at this time is the suggestion that the first ministers' conference in Canada be institutionalized. That makes a lot of sense.
To say that these proposals are not new is accurate, but 1 do not, in so saying that, mean in any sense to denigrate them. No country in the world at any period in the past or the present could conceive of dealing with a package of constitutional proposals that were primarily new. By definition, a constitution for a people has to represent a kind of serious level of consensus building. It has to reflect in a serious way the aspirations, the values, the objectives in a political context of people at a given time. Therefore, these proposals that have been made by the Prime Minister, by the government of the day, while not new, are relevant and are good and are, for us, acceptable in principle. 1 hope they can be speedily dealt with in terms of getting acceptance by the committee, and ultimately by the Parliament of Canada.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that what we do find to be new, and significantly new in this package of proposals which is not only unacceptable to us but disturbingly unacceptable, and in that regard I am referring to the proposed replacement for the second chamber of the parliamentary system, is the new House of the Federation. I say, and 1 say it in all seriousness, that if the government had deliberately set out to propose an institution that would simultaneously promote discontent, fractionalize the country, and frustrate the democratic will, it could not have done better than propose the House of the Federation. 1 say this without any attitude of partisanship on this question and with no exaggerated sense, in fact no sense at all of being negative.
The Prime Minister indicated in his discussion this afternoon an approach of flexibility on this and on other matters. I want to stress that what I am about to say will be in like vein, with the same openness of mind, to be persuaded, ultimately by the government if my arguments turn out to be fallacious, and we can be shown, on the basis of experience in other countries or on the logic of the system as l see it being proposed, as a mistake in judgment, then my party and I would be prepared to reconsider.
So the attitude on this fundamental question it seems to me has to be open on all sides of the House. With that in mind I make the following criticisms. Simply stated, if we create what 1 regard as a kind of abomination, for the first time in modern

history we will have a body as a second chamber with even more powers than the existing Senate, but this power will be used. That is a fundamental concern, or ought to be a fundamental concern, not only for Canadians now but for our future Canadians. The inevitable consequence, in my judgment, of the proposal that has been made by the government will be a deadlock in democracy in our country. A triumph ultimately of the second chamber over the House of Commons is the exact reversal of the principle of parliamentary democracy, which is that the House of Commons should remain supreme in all legislative processes. The House of Commons is the body directly elected by the people of Canada, the democratic body in the system.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, we cannot allow this suggestion to be implemented as it stands. I will not go through all the details. However, we know there will be 118 members, almost half of the total coming as a result of federal elections in proportion to the party vote at the national level, the other half coming at various times corresponding to the popular party vote in a given provincial election. The duration of the tenure of the members, of both federal nominees and provincial nominees, will vary according to the duration of the various legislatures. In short, we will have a great change-over in membership. In comparison with the existing institution this might be welcome, but welcome only on first analysis. I say this because it signifies the kind of people we would get in this new body, if it comes into being. These men and women would come there in anticipation of acting. They would not only have that anticipation but would carry it out. They would not be there very long but while they are in Ottawa, coming from all over the country, they would propose to act and indeed would act as legislators.
The powers of this body are, if anything, greater than the existing powers of the Senate of Canada. In addition to the normal powers, they would have the right to appoint or play a role in approving nominees to the Supreme Court of Canada and to other key federal bodies. In the normal legislative process they would have the right to introduce bills of all kinds, with the exception of money bills. They would have this right, and significantly and crucially from our argument, they would have the right to frustration, that is, to stop the passage of any bill, including money bills, that come from the House of Commons. Once this is done it would take a two thirds vote in the House of Commons, with certain exceptions-the Prime Minister is shaking his head and I suspect I will come to a certain aspect of the argument that he is shaking his head about in a moment-to overcome this decision by the second body.
What is wrong with this proposed system? It would achieve exactly what the Fathers of Confederation 111 years ago intended for the Senate. We rarely read it in our school books, but without exception, Cartier, Macdonald, D'Arcy McGee, all said that the principal task of the Senate was to inhibit this pernicious force known as democracy which was emanating from the United States. There are a number of quotations, hardly the kind one would look on with a great deal of pride if
June 27, 1978

one has a solid commitment to democracy, that make it clear that in addition to the representational role for the provinces, the Fathers of Confederation clearly had it in mind that the Senate of Canada, not being elected as was established about 100 years earlier in the United States directly by the people, was to be an inhibiting factor in the democratic process. Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, it did not turn out that way with the existing Senate for a variety of reasons, principally because the Senate turned out to be the fiefdom of the prime minister of the day and it was widely known and widely accepted that the day the Senate overturned legislation, certainly in recent decades, as passed by this House, within a matter of days if not hours, steps would be undertaken that would lead to the abolition of the Senate.
My concern is that this new creation proposed by the government would act effectively as a check on democracy, a check on the will of the people of Canada expressed in a federal election to elect the House of Commons.
Let me give a concrete example of my expressed general concern. 1 met with an official of the government, perhaps the leading constitutional official who, no doubt at the instigation of the Prime Minister, was playing a role with the Leader of the Opposition and myself the day the bill was introduced, in order to explain some of the technical details of it. During the course of this meeting I pointed out that, as I understand it, the present Senate, as a result of the most recent election, would be dominated by members of the opposition, the Conservative Party of Canada and the NDP, and the Liberals would have a minority. This was easily ascertained in terms of the voting records in recent elections.
The crucial point I put to him was that my understanding of the law as it would pertain to this new body was that, had it been in existence at the time, it could have held up the AIB legislation brought forward by this government a couple of years ago. 1 pointed out that a central proposal affecting, in the government's view, the good of the country, something that ought to have been done rather quickly, according to the government, could have been held up for as much as six months by that body. The reply I received from the senior official was yes, it could happen.
I asked why that would not happen. The reply I received was indicative of a number of people who are supporting this kind of body. He said that somehow these people would be reasonable, would sense the mood of the country, and would not respond in an inhibiting way when the House of Commons spoke clearly.
I have rarely heard a more naive view about the working of an electoral system. It is the height of naivete to assume that a newly created body, which is going to be based directly on proportional party votes in the provinces in half measure, and the other half on proportional party votes in the federal election, would automatically, especially when they are men and women in parties on the opposite side of the government, act with the same assumption about what the national interest
The Constitution
is as the government of the day. With perfectly good conscience and perfectly good integrity, they would almost inevitably do the opposite.
In a party system in Canada the people respond in terms of the collective set of values of their party. They inevitably look at a situation from a party perspective. Therefore a national program brought in by a democratically elected House of Commons, and I used the example of the AIB, could be thwarted by that other body, not for weeks but for many months. In that situation the government would find itself, on issue after issue, stymied by a majority opposition in the other place.
I have no doubt at all that deadlock and delay would result. The practical concerns of Canadians at any given period of time, whether it is job creation, regional insecurity, housing, fishing, consumer rights or whatever, those legislative measures which should be produced rather quickly in a democratic age to meet the needs of the people, would be frustrated and held up by this body.
The result would be that instead of reducing tensions in this country produced by regional discontent, this new body would exacerbate them. It could lead to a sense of frustration with federal politics on a national scale that could be truly alarming at some point in the future. Perhaps that is why the Prime Minister was shaking his head earlier. I do not know.
If the government says that it assumes a government of the day would invoke the proposed urgency clause in the legislation to head off delays, I say it simply has not thought through its own proposals carefully enough. If that is the intention, the whole purpose of this newly created second chamber will seem to be simply a charade.
The conclusion is inescapable. The body could use its powers, and I am inclined to think it would, and frustrate the democratic will. Or not use them; in that event it would be seen to be a completely phony institution, fully equivalent to our existing Senate. It would play no real role in the world of power in Ottawa, which the Prime Minister in his comments this afternoon quite correctly described as being a central concern of the regions of Canada.
Everyone outside of 25 miles of Dundas and Yonge in downtown Toronto feels like a regional Canadian. All those Canadians have some sense that they are not getting their say in the legitimate legal power structure in Ottawa. I say that this proposal from the government is the last kind we should be considering to meet those needs.
An additional negative result of this body would be that it would undermine the potentially creative role played by the first ministers' meetings. I mentioned earlier that 1 was pleased to see in the proposals the suggestion that the first ministers' meetings be institutionalized, that a meeting take place at least once a year. I think that makes good sense.
The premiers of our provinces, unlike their equivalents in the United States, Switzerland, West Germany and Australia, have real power. They have much more power than the heads of the Australian states, the American states, the cantons in

June 27, 1978
The Constitution
Switzerland or lander in Germany. They have to play an integral role in the governing of this country, particularly in areas of overlapping federal-provincial concern. Therefore the proposal to have the meetings regularized is a good one.
The practice initiated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in discussing proposals for his most recent budget, although there was a significant bungling in the middle of it, was, as I said at the time, a commendable initiative and something that should be duplicated. The more that can be done in terms of this kind of federal-provincial recognition of the real powers which our provinces have, the better.
I suggest to the Prime Minister, however, that this body would undermine the good intentions of the recommendation that first ministers' conferences be institutionalized. It would not only thwart the democratic will of the House of Commons in Ottawa, but would undermine the role played by the provincial premiers, either when they meet alone to make proposals or when they meet with the Prime Minister of the day.
The third concern we have about this new body is the double majority principle, an idea borrowed from Calhoun, one to which we should give long, hesitant consideration. The Charter of Rights, including linguistic rights, is a good idea and is embodied solidly in the proposed new constitution. So I ask, Mr. Speaker, why do we need this new proposal of a double majority based, as it is, on racial differences? I simply say that my colleagues and 1 want to look at that question with a great deal of care because its very existence could be a source of significant disunity in the future.
1 want to deal with the regional concerns which are at the heart of the sole significant new proposal. I refer, of course, to the proposed House of the Federation. The Prime Minister expressed his concern about it this afternoon. First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that for me the concerns of the regions are primarily economic. They are primarily dependent upon national and provincial political leadership which sets out the right kind of economic priorities. Having said that, it would be to misunderstand reality to see no role at all for constitutional procedures of the government in coming to grips with those regional differences. That is why federal states have been created around the world, including our own.
On behalf of my party, Mr. Speaker, I wish to put forward a proposal which seems to me deals in a much more fundamental and adequate way in meeting the terms of democracy and the requirements of regionalism than is embodied in the government's proposed second chamber. Instead of that abomination which has been proposed, it seems to me serious consideration should be given to the following: instead of setting up a new body with 118 members, take perhaps 100 of them, divide them into five to coincide with the number of economic regions throughout the country so that there would be 20 or so from each of those economic regions. I am using the 20 or 100 as approximate figures. These people would be

elected, on the basis of proportional party votes in the regions, directly to the House of Commons.
Instead of setting up a second chamber on the line proposed by the Prime Minister, my idea is that we would take 100 people who would be proposed in a series of party lists in each of the regions so that citizens in every part of Canada could see, submitted by each of the parties, a list of outstanding individuals whom the parties are proposing as candidates for those parties in that region. So there would be added approximately 100 seats to those already in the House of Commons. Their holders would constitute a genuine representative force from the regions, and they would be indirectly elected by the people in those regions.
What would be the advantages of such a system?
The Prime Minister smiles.

I say to the smiling Prime Minister, who tends to take that attitude toward any idea which comes from sources outside his own party, that the advantages would, in our humble view, be as follows: first, Atlantic Canada, the prairies, and British Columbia would gain proportionately in representation in this House. These are the regions which, for understandable geographic and economic reasons, feel they have less input into the conduct of this country's affairs than they should, less sense of identification with the decisions which are made here. They would have a greater say. To this extent, their increased representation would constitute a contribution to national unity.
Second, all parties in this House would virtually be represented in each region as a result of so many being elected on a proportional basis. This, in my view, would lead to a marked improvement in the caucus discussions of all the parties because they would more adequately reflect the diverse nature of our country. In addition, the government of the day would be relieved of some of the problems the present government faces. For example, it wanted a representative from Alberta and had to persuade a Tory member to join its caucus in order to get one.
By the process I am suggesting, the government of the day, whatever its political complexion, would have among its ranks not only competent men and women but, hopefully, since the party itself had prepared the lists, an outstanding man or woman, presumably of cabinet quality, at its disposition. That is regional input where it really counts in a democratic system. Regional influence would be felt directly in the caucuses of the parties of the House of Commons and directly in the cabinet of Canada.
Another advantage of this idea which I am submitting for consideration is this: the number I am proposing would be significantly smaller than the total composition of the House of Commons. The vast majority of the members would still be representing individual constituencies. The Prime Minister did not deal with this aspect when he was discussing the various alternatives-the only point he made about the House of Commons reflecting regional needs related to the election of all members by a PR system. As he knows, a number of other
June 27, 1978

countries combine the two methods, right in the lower house there are members representing single constituencies and members elected by proportional representation.
The advantage of my proposal, it seems to me, is that the vast majority of the members would still represent constituencies, something which 1 believe to be very desirable in a democracy since the majority of the men and women who are elected have direct contact with the people and a direct opportunity to respond to the needs of given groups of electors. But there would be a significant minority element which would provide important and, in many cases, decisive regional input into the decision making processes of the House of Commons and of the cabinet.
Moreover, such an arrangement would not fly in the face of parliamentary democracy as I believe the other proposal does. It would be in accord with the tradition of parliamentary democracy that the House of Commons should be the ascendant body and that the cabinet should be responsible to the House of Commons. This would not be the case if the proposal for a House of Federation were adopted. The course presently proposed would undermine the authority of the House of Commons. I hope that not only the government but the official opposition will seriously consider the idea 1 have put forward.
1 want in my concluding comments to turn away from the constitution. I said earlier that the principal sources of discontent in our land are not constitutional in origin. 1 strongly believe this. They have not had their origins in the maldistribution of constitutional power or other related legal matters which are inextricably connected with provincial and federal jurisdictional matters.
One hundred and eleven years ago the Fathers of Confederation talked about creating what became Canada. They did not restrict themselves in those discussions to technical, legal matters. They talked about the broadest essential purposes of nationhood. They understood that a constitution was to be a means, not an end in itself. At that time there was regional economic concern among the provinces in Atlantic Canada, and in Upper Canada and Lower Canada. A very real concern was expressed about the possibilities and opportunities for economic growth and expansion which would inevitably entail a crossing of this continent. In short, the problems were economic. Regional economics were an essential and central part of the confederation debates. They were a concern then. They are a concern today, and they are not related to the constitution.
Also at that time there was a concern among the provinces which were coming together to form the Dominion of Canada about domination by the United States. It was very real among all the delegates who gathered to discuss the future of Canada. I submit that that same concern is or ought to be uppermost in the minds of serious politicians today in Canada. That too is a non-constitutional matter.
One hundred and eleven years ago it was recognized that the principal means of ensuring French-speaking Canadians the
The Constitution
survival of their culture was the creation of a province in which they would be the numerical majority and in which, through the democratic process, they would be able to ensure-within a united Canada which would protect them for other reasons and which would ensure growth for other reasons-the continued development of their own language and culture. That aspect of the constitution existed 111 years ago. That aspect exists today. That aspect, therefore, is a non-constitutional concern for us today. In fact, I suspect that perhaps the one permanent accomplishment of the Parti Quebecois in the history of the province of Quebec will be the ultimate establishment of the supremacy and the sense of legitimacy and domination of the French language in every aspect of Quebec life. But that was done within the existing constitution.
There is in the history of a nation, our nation as well as any others, matters which completely transcend legal or constitutional discussion. They are economic and cultural in nature, and they are matters to which the government of the day has not addressed itself. The government of the day has failed in coming to grips with them, and to that extent the government must be held responsible for failing to generate the kinds of opportunities which could come in terms of economic growth.
In western Canada changes are needed to produce a system in the prairies whereby they could develop their secondary industry. Changes are needed in the freight rate system, and those changes would be policy economic decisions. Regional economic development in Atlantic Canada involves policy economic decisions and not constitutional decisions. So, the question of national economic independence for the country as a whole is a broad national economic matter, and again the government of the day has given worse than no attention to that important consideration.
What I am saying is that we support a number of the proposals which have been made-

Order, please. 1 regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired. He may continue with unanimous consent. Does the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) have unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the extra time. I will be brief.
We support a number of the key proposals which are in the proposed legislation. We look forward to discussing them in detail at the committee stage. We categorically reject the idea of a House of the Federation but are submitting an alternative for consideration which we think would much more adequately and democratically deal with the regional needs and concerns of the country. However, above and beyond that we are saying that the basic concerns of French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians at this point in our history, as indeed was the case 111 years ago, have almost no connection with constitutional matters. They have every connection with the question

June 27, 1978
The Constitution
of economic and cultural leadership, and that more than anything else is required in this country.
Before I sit down I want to move an amendment which pertains to that other place which has been centred so much in the discussions so far today in the House. We believe that a matter as important as the Constitution of Canada should certainly be determined directly by the people who are elected by the people of Canada. We do not believe that future constitutional arrangements of this country should be determined, even in broad outline, by people who, as I said earlier, happen to be the fiefdom of the prime minister of the day or his predecessor. We categorically reject, therefore, the idea that members of the other place, the Senate, should be on such an important committee as this one is in the history of our country?
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended,
(a)	by deleting from the first paragraph thereof the words "a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons" and by substituting therefor the words "a Special Committee of the House of Commons";
(b)	by deleting from the second paragraph thereof the words "on the part of this House"; and
(c)	by inserting a period after the words "within Canada" in the fourth paragraph and by deleting all of the fifth paragraph from the said motion.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: Order, please. It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be debated at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert)- Manpower-Employment of immigrants; the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp)-Abortion-Request for review of abortion laws; the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen)-Abortion-Funding of abortion clinics.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, we are perhaps entering today the most important debate in the last 100 years, during which discussion has been going on between the representatives of different Canadian provinces. At that time, Canada did not exist. There were Upper Canada and Lower Canada and the colonies, the present maritime provinces, and I think that since that time many things have been said and written about the constitution. Lately, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) submitted to us a bill on the reform of the constitution and we are asked today to adopt a motion for the creation of a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to discuss the bill on the reform of the constitution and report to parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I doubt that such a committee on the constitution is necessary because a few years ago, in 1970, the House of Commons created a Special Joint Parliamentary Committee on the Constitution of Canada. That committee went all over Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, to find out what the Canadian citizens of every province and territory wanted. It visited all the provinces and 47 of the most important Canadian centres and gathered, in extraordinary quantities, testimonies of all kinds dealing with the constitutional problem and the ideas expressed by Canadian citizens, both Anglophone and Francophone, as well as Canadians of other ethnic origins. Those people contributed their ideas about what a new constitution should say. A report was tabled in the House in 1972; I

June 27, 1978

have a feeling it was put on a shelf, where all it does it take up room in a library.
Mr. Speaker, the travelling expenses of that committee across Canada amounted to between $3 million and $4 million and, today, it is suggested that another special joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate be set up to travel to almost the same places, meet just about the same people, to get almost the same information that we already have in the report on the constitution of Canada.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I have doubts about the need for that committee but, having heard the speeches of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), I have a feeling that they seem to agree on the setting up of such a committee, which committee will, in any event, be created to study anew that constitutional problem. It goes without saying that it is indeed true that the problem is extremely important, and that it must be looked into, in every aspect.
Mr. Speaker, there is another point that surprised me as well as the members of my party-because this afternoon I am speaking on behalf of the Social Credit Party of Canada and it is that this resolution proposes the setting up of a joint committee on the first phase of that constitutional amendment which precisely provides for the abolition of the Senate. Mr. Speaker, I and we, of the Social Credit Party of Canada, agree entirely with the amendment introduced by the Leader of the New Democratic Party to the effect that that committee be made up only of elected members of the House of Commons whose responsibility it would be to examine the issue of rewriting the main part of the Constitution of Canada dealing with the federal administration which is being proposed in the white paper introduced a few days ago and in the constitutional amendment bill.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the representatives of parliament should be the ones to consider this bill and meet with the Canadian public since it seems that it has now been decided to meet with the Canadian public to hear their opinions. Notwithstanding the decision that will be made following that committee report and the rejection of the bill introduced by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last week, I believe at that time the senators will have to accept the decision made by the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment of the constitution is nothing new, and the culminating point I believe in that discussion arrives at a time when the national unity crisis seems at its highest point since the beginning of the federation. It seems that the party now heading this government-and it has been running it for several years-has a lot of things to blame itself for with respect to the events that occurred in Canada over the past ten or 15 years. I think we have every reason to blame severely this federal government because as the political authority in this country it promoted and brought about the national harmony crisis in Canada. They talk of national unity in a country which is made up not only of English Canadians and French Canadians but also a host of other nationalities and to try to make a united Canada out of all those diverse
The Constitution
groups I believe is to daydream. We should rather talk about and try to harmonize all those cultural diversities to make a nation out of them. I think I could use here a musical image. For example, you can take a band of 20, 25 or 30 different musical instruments that have no resemblance and produce different sounds, and when you can put them together in harmony, you get melodies which are truly pleasant to listen to.
Mr. Speaker, if we do the same thing with all the nationalities which make up Canada we might build a truly strong nation, the kind of country we would like to have. I think that all Canadians in all parts of the country, maybe with a few exceptions on both sides of the linguistic border in Canada, wish to live in a strong nation but they also wish that each and every province making up Canada be strong and able to administer itself as it sees fit.
The Social Credit Party of Canada has long since been warning Canadians about the strictly strategic position of the federal government. Through its attitude, it has allowed the crisis to develop and then tried to make people believe that the same government would solve the crisis through amendments like these. Mr. Speaker, 1 have been sitting here since 1962 and I and several of my colleagues from Quebec, like our late leader Real Caouette, have taken every opportunity to urge that Canada be given a constitution recognizing certain rights for every province and not only for Quebec. I remember particularly that during the general election the Progressive Conservative party had proposed two nations as an alternative. In the province of Quebec at least, that party did not receive the approval of Canadians on that subject and was practically wiped out. In the sixties Quebec had a Union nationale government which in some respects was closely identified with the Progressive Conservative party and the leader of that government, Mr. Daniel Johnson, was also proposing the two nations alternative. We know what happened to the Union nationale in a provincial election-they disappeared completely from the electoral map of the province of Quebec.
The Social Credit Party of Canada has always claimed- and our former leader Real Caouette mentioned it several times in this House as well as in public tribunes throughout Canada-that our party was for a single Canadian nation, two official languages and multiculturalism precisely because Canada is composed of different nationalities which largely contribute to enhance the character of Canada and we must respect those ethnic entities.
Mr. Speaker, in the face of this constitution which we are being asked to reform, I think we must be very careful. In this first phase, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is proposing that we study only-or almost uniquely if you want-sections of the constitution dealing exclusively with the federal administration and in this regard the Prime Minister believes that the provinces have no say in what is already ascribed to the federal government by the present constitution. Mr. Speaker, I think we must be very careful in that respect. It is not

June 27, 1978
The Constitution
quite true that the provinces have no right to voice their point of view about what comes under the federal administration. There may be some aspects which the provinces would like to see fall under their jurisdiction. To my mind, that is where the provinces should be given the privilege of deciding whether these sections of the constitution should be kept under federal jurisdiction or whether they should be reassigned to the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, if the provinces are to respect the constitution they must participate in its drafting without constraints, they must decide among themselves what they want to have administered by the central government and what they want to administer themselves. Only then could a province be said to act less than graciously if it did not respect a constitution to which it would have been a party. During a convention held in Drummondville, the Social Credit Party of Canada passed resolutions dealing with the Canadian constitution or the reform of the Canadian constitution and these resolutions have been ratified at a council or at a national convention held in Winnipeg. Mr. Speaker, what the Social Credit Party of Canada is asking for is a constitutional amendment which would allow the provinces to participate in the drafting of a constitution the same way the provinces participated in the creation of the Canadian federation in 1867. In the first phase:
Each province will have to institute a process of public consultation enabling all individuals, associations, groups or public bodies to express their views regarding the constitution. Second, in light of this first round of consultation, each provincial government will have to submit its proposal for a constitutional formula to the people of the province for their approval by way of a referendum. Third, when every province would have been given a mandate by its people, the provincial governments would initiate interprovincial negotiations on a basis of equality, that is the provinces or the government of the provinces would meet to negotiate among themselves without particiption by the federal government. Fourth, the conclusions of these negotiations should be submitted a second time to the people of every province by way of a referendum and no province would be bound to accept them by virtue of their right to self-determination.
Finally, following the results of this consultation by referendum, the provincial authorities will ask the federal government to take all legal, political and administrative steps to respect the wishes of the provincial governments, duly elected by their constituents. Mr. Speaker, in a letter dated June 12, 1968, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada wrote to the premier of Quebec and said among other things:
This renewal will give us the occasion to provide Canada with a new constitution which will remedy the deficiencies and drawbacks of the one we have been living with since 1867 and which will ratify a new pact between all citizens of Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if we want to ratify a new pact between all Canadian citizens, it must be by referendum, it was not done in 1867, and maybe this is one of the wrongs of this constitution. But if we want this constitution to be recognized,

accepted and respected, not only by the provinces but by all Canadians, I think we must give them the opportunity to decide, through a referendum, whether they want to accept the provincial proposals regarding what should be administered by the federal government and by the provinces. Mr. Speaker, if it is a renewed, amended or entirely new constitution that we are seeking for the next 50 to 100 years, then this constitution must stand on a solid foundation and that requires going to the Canadian people.
There is an aspect of the Prime Minister's proposal on constitutional reform which deals specifically with the representation or the changes in the Senate. It is proposed to abolish the Senate and to replace it with a House of Federation whose members would be partially appointed by the federal government and partially by the provinces. That is perhaps an improvement over what we have known so far in terms of appointment of senators, but I think, Mr. Speaker, that if we want a Senate that is truly representative not only of the regions of Canada but of all Canadians, we must go much further than what the constitutional reform bill proposes. Such a Senate could, in my view, be appointed partially by the federal government, partially by the provinces and partially by public bodies. It would then represent in some way Canadian corporations and public bodies, of which I could name a few, for example, the Canadian Federation of Municipalities, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the workers' unions, union-management associations, chambers of commerce, the Canadian Bar, the College of Physicians and so on. Those corporations could be called upon to appoint senators, and since of course they do not change as frequently as do federal or provincial governments-which could bring about rather frequent re-shuffles in the Senate personnel set up along the lines of this proposal-the participation of public corporations would I believe stabilize considerably the Senate chamber, and stabilize it to such an extent that they could be given the task not only of monitoring the legislations brought forward by the Canadian parliament, but most of all to deal with commissions of inquiry, for example. So I think we could get a truly representative Senate made up of men from all walks of life who could do efficient services with regard to commissions of inquiry and replace those we already know, which operate at tremendous costs and which we could dispense with since we would already have the people needed to undertake the same studies and inquiries.
Mr. Speaker, if the right hon. Prime Minister is looking for ideas, here is one which is not put forward lightly. The Social Credit Party of Canada is not the only one making suggestions, for I know that the public bodies have already done so, and I am making representations on their behalf calling on hon. members to seriously consider this method of appointing senators.
Mr. Speaker, there are other peculiarities in this bill which have caught my attention, and evidently for lack of time, I do not think I shall be able to examine every point. There is one,
June 27, 1978

however, on which I should like to devote a few minutes, for I think it is very important. In the section which deals with political and legal rights and freedoms within the constitution,

Well, Mr. Speaker, it is all very nice to talk about rights, but rights without powers do not mean much. Mr. Speaker, I think we should add to the constitution something that would allow all Canadians not only to have some rights but also the power to translate those rights into reality, the power to use and enjoy their own property. We talk about conflicts between capitalists and socialists. I for one would like all Canadians to be capitalists and to have their own home in Canada. I see a Canadian constitution granting these rights through the powers it would give to each and every Canadian. No matter what kind of constitution we give ourselves, if it does not provide that assurance to all Canadians, they will never respect it because too many of them will be right in questioning the value of their country, their government and their parliament.

We cannot count on the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) to keep a tight hand on the corporation. We know that from past experience. In fact, we find it wondrously strange that this minister, who at one time said he was the guardian of private enterprise and free enterprise and who was the champion of the free enterprise system, has not only joined the socialist Liberal government which has been ruling this country for ten years but also now is one of the stoutest advocates of government intervention, including the type of financing he is sponsoring through the EDC. The EDC agrees to throw in all the interests, take all the accumulated interest and principal, and sign a new note. That way it looks current to the EDC as well as to the country involved, and everyone is happy. Mr. MacDonald was saying that each of those countries had had one or more reschedulings. When he says that, it is interesting to note that some countries have been rescheduled more than once. They will do it one year, and if they still fall into default, they will do it the second year. In the years from 1964 through to the present time it gives the gross amount rescheduled-

-a further extension, and we have $38 million outstanding at the moment.

Let me clarify here. I am not suggesting that the corporation is necessarily legally obligated. What I am saying is that it has certainly given encouragement and, if you like, moral commitments to various people to make extensive financial arrangements, and if it even lived up to only half of the so-called moral commitments, it would be way over the authorization that either this or the previous parliament has given to the corporation.

Mr. Hegan, who is vice president of finance for EDC, responded by saying:
Yes, Mr. Stevens. On what we have discussed at this juncture, that is correct. As I said in the introductory remarks, the character of our commitments will follow very closely the credit-worthiness characteristics and the efforts of Canadian exporters. One would find amongst the countries with oil revenues and some of the eastern European countries a strong credit-worthiness.
Let us put that into perspective. I have said that they have run over, certainly in moral commitments, the authorizations that parliament had given them, and not only have they run over those authorizations but they have done so to the extent of about $2.7 billion in favour of communist and OPEC nations. Surely a committee of the House should have the right to inquire to what degree the EDC is right in extending that kind of financing to a communist state. Communist states function in an entirely different way as far as their labour structure and wage scales are concerned. Consequently, by our encouraging development in some of those communist states, we are encouraging further unfair competition with our own producers in Canada. 1 will come back to that a little later.
The other thing we have to ask ourselves is to what extent should we, as EDC has been doing and proposes to do, be lending money to OPEC nations? Has the government totally forgotten that Canada is a nation which is running up significant current account deficits with the world, whereas the OPEC nations are running up huge current account surpluses? Let me put it into perspective, Mr. Speaker. We have a Crown agency proposing to lend hundreds of millions, even up into the billions, of dollars to the OPEC nations. These nations in 1974 had a current account surplus in the aggregate of $70.5 billion. In 1975 they had a current account surplus of $39.5 billion and in 1976 it was $41 billion. This figure was repeated generally in 1977. The figures which 1 have been referring to do not come from the government, but from where we get so much of our detailed economic information, the international economic report of the president of the United States transmitted to Congress in January of last year.
The point I am trying to make is that when we are dealing with a corporation which has requested authorization of $26 billion, it behooves this parliament to ensure that if they are granted any such authorization they are required to return to a committee of this House to give an accounting of their activities at least once a year, such as I am suggesting in motion No. 5. I say that because how else can you get some type of perspective into EDC or at least an explanation for the

Canadian public as to why it feels justitied in loaning nunareus of millions of dollars to OPEC nations which have current account surpluses of the magnitude I have been referring to, while we are running current account deficits of something over $4 billion per year.
I say that because I feel that so much could be done to help domestic industries with at least part of the money EDC is proposing to lend various countries around the world. Let me put it this way, Mr. Speaker. The fishermen on our east and west coasts need financing to help refurbish their fishing fleets. Money is needed to build the Bay of Fundy project, and more money is needed to develop the hydroelectric potential in the lower Churchill and in Labrador. And we all know that Montreal is still without proper sewage treatment facilities. These funds could be used to complete such projects as these.
There is also the Toronto area urban transportation problem. The Toronto area, Mr. Speaker, an area that I am familiar with, is a startling example of the inconsistencies of this government. In Toronto we need $58 million to help in the realignment of trackage coming in from the west of Toronto to Union Station. We cannot put any more commuter trains on the lines without that realignment. Railways are a federal responsibility and yet to date the government in Ottawa has consistently refused to lend or in any other way provide the $58 million which is needed for that realignment on the west side of Toronto.
Does it make sense that we have a government which says there are no funds available to help commuters get to and from work in the Toronto area and yet have a Crown corporation which is proposing to put out hundreds of millions of dollars that in many cases will help to build transportation facilities in foreign countries? I see that the minister is in the House, and I wish, before this debate concludes at the report stage, that he would get up and at least offer the government's explanation as to why there should be funds available to help people in other countries with their transportation needs but no funds available to help, for example, the commuters in the Toronto area with their transportation needs.
I know that the justification for much of the Export Development Corporation activities is the hope that they will create jobs in Canada. But would it not be doubly advantageous if we could not only create jobs in Canada but, in creating those jobs, build some of the infrastructures we need in this country, such as the commuter type of transportation facility which is needed to help our own people in their own livelihoods?
I would like now to go to the Canadian west. The grain handling facilities have needed improvement in efficiency for years. In many areas farmers have to leave the grain in the fields in the hope that they can get it off early enough in spring to avoid the rains and subsequent rotting. As we know, British Columbia would like to revitalize its pulp and paper industry. But to such projects as these Ottawa states that there are no funds available or very limited funds. However, the government seems to have funds to help countries like Poland, Cuba,
Export Development Act
Iran, Romania, the United States and even Russia with similar projects which are being completed in those countries.
The $26 billion package the government is proposing to award in this bill to EDC represents more than 10 per cent of all the goods and services produced in Canada this year. That is the magnitude of the figures we are talking about. To put it another way, the $26 billion is approximately two and a half times the total federal budget a mere ten years ago. For one Crown corporation to have such authority is unbelievable, but to have such authority without the proper scrutiny of a committee of this House is irresponsible. That is why I am proposing in motion No. 5 that there be this reference at least once a year to somehow police EDC activities.
Some of my colleagues have pointed out that not only is the bill proposing to give EDC this massive authorization, but there is nothing in it to prevent the corporation from loaning money to the very nations which are going to use those funds to become more competitive with us in international trade in subsequent years.
My colleagues have mentioned the $160 million loan for a pulp and paper mill in Poland, money the EDC put up despite the fact that our own pulp and paper industry is struggling to stay alive in the face of increased competition abroad, and despite the fact that everyone expects the Polish people to be one of our major competitors in the European paper market.
EDC has rationalized this decision by pointing out that Poland would buy Canadian equipment for its plant. However, this just does not hold up because in a state run society, as I have already mentioned, the Polish worker is paid far less than his Canadan counterpart, and ultimately Poland will be able to undercut Canadian prices. The pulp and paper industry, which is operating at something like 75 per cent capacity now, will be hurt even more, costing thousands of Canadian jobs.
The Polish loan is only the tip of the iceberg. The EDC, for reasons of its own, seems bent on clobbering this industry. Recent EDC projects include loans of $102.6 million for a forestry development in Iran, $57 million for paper mill projects for Argentina, and still more millions for pulp and paper concerns in Peru and Romania.
And the United States.

As the hon. member points out, they are also putting money into the United States to help build steel mills and pulp and paper facilities there. The EDC is putting up $400 million to help others compete with our forest industry. The government, it seems, expects Canadians to help everybody but themselves.
Just recently I spoke to the president of a pulp and paper concern. This company in fact was referred to in the hearings before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. He pointed out that the financing the EDC is extending to other pulp and paper concerns all over the world is so favourable that if his company wished to build comparable facilites in Canada there is no way they could get

He also pointed out that if the company wished to extend or modernize their pulp and paper facilities, they were in the ludicrous position of having to go to other countries to see if they could get the same financial treatment that EDC is giving to foreign concerns. This would put them back in a competitive position while the EDC pursues its financing activity in foreign countries. Surely at some point the minister will see how ludicrous the situation has become where industry after industry is basically selling state financing as opposed to selling their goods.
The unfortunate thing is that while one year's work may be gained now, 15 or 20 years ahead the Canadian public will pay heavily when today's borrowers default on these loans. We have been a source of ready and cheap money for projects in the United States, in Russia, in the oil rich nations of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Iran and Venezuela. In fact, by the end of 1976 EDC had loaned a total of $275.8 million to the Arab bloc and oil exporting countries, and this year it granted Algeria a staggering line of credit of $1.2 billion.
If hon. members are interested in what Algeria is doing with our money, which is relatively long-term funding at a low interest rate, they should read the current edition of The Economist, the British magazine. If they do, however, they will not sleep tonight. The Algerians are proposing to invest that money and make 180 per cent on it as they develop their petrochemical resources.
Has sanity been lost in this country, Mr. Speaker? We are told that we do not have sufficient funds to develop the tar sands and Arctic gas resources, but apparently we have a $1.2 billion line of credit that can be made available to Algeria to develop their natural resources, such as gas, at a profit to them of 180 per cent. This is another example of why we would like a reference to a committee of this House in order to get this thing aired at least once a year.
Imagine, Mr. Speaker, at the end of 1976 the OPEC nations had accumulated more than $45 billion in trade surpluses while Canada hobbled along with a current account deficit of $4 billion per year, and if you aggregate that it is about $16 billion. Yet we are loaning them money. We are in deficit while they are in substantial surplus.
Equally perplexing are the loans to Cuba, Russia, Bulgaria, Romania and other communist countries. It is no doubt desirable to encourage trade with the east, but must we subsidize it with low-cost loans, on average at about 8 per cent interest, while our own industries are forced to pay much higher rates or cannot even get money? Would it not be much better if the government invested at least a portion of this $26 billion at home where we need jobs, where industry needs a hand and many infrastructure projects should be completed to help our commuters get to work in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, or Edmonton? Our fishermen need new fleets to enable them to haul better catches and farmers in the west need better facilities to help harvest their crops. That is why we would like a committee review of the activities of the EDC. It cannot be left with the authorizations that are proposed in this bill without tighter scrutiny by a suitable committee of this House.

I see my time is almost up and I want to give others an opportunity to speak on my amendment if they so desire. But this situation is serious, Mr. Speaker. In five to ten years Canadians will be asking why there was such negligence in 1977 and 1978-why authorizations were granted so irresponsibly to the Export Development Corporation without better scrutiny by parliamentarians.
That is what is at stake, Mr. Speaker. That is why I urge hon. members to support my suggestion that there be a permanent reference to a standing committee of this House to ensure that we have an ongoing scrutiny of the activities of the EDC. What we are asking for is not unique. There is a permanent reference with respect to Air Canada's activities and whose annual report will be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications on an yearly basis. Surely if it is right for Air Canada it should also be right for the Export Development Corporation, which will become one of the major Crown corporations of Canada if not the largest.
That is the case I should like to put in support of my amendment as set out in motion No. 5. I will have more to say about motion No. 6 and possibly I will speak again on third reading, but I urge all hon. members not to accept the EDC bill lightly. In future, they are going to be called to account for any irresponsibilities of the present time. I caution them that those irresponsibilities will surface if we do not ensure that there is proper committee review of this corporation's activities such as I have suggested.
