With no taxes, the hon. member says. But there is the concept, Mr. Speaker, of money-grubbing, making money, profiteering. These people are the same ones who will stand up and argue that they are really trying to help third world countries deal with their economic problems. One would say that they are trying to take advantage of third world countries and make all these millions of dollars.
The way in which the EDC goes about this whole business of lending money in the international market is a real concern. From time to time there is a useful editorial in the Northern Miner on the mining industry. Even though I take a subscription to it, I do not use this paper as my handbook for speech making or comments on the mining industry. However, if one is selective it can be put to use. One has to assume the people who write the Northern Miner and who contribute to it have some knowledge of the mining industry and have some concern about the way in which we develop this industry in Canada.
In this connection I quote from the Northern Miner of November 3, 1977. The following appeared in their editorial of that date:
Although Guatemala and Indonesia cannot be charged with having precipitated the current situation-
The "current situation" means the lay-offs of workers in the Sudbury basin. The editorial goes on to say:
-looking further down the road to the years when nickel markets improve, the reality is that there will be more nickel producers laying a claim to a share of the nickel market. And no amount of castigation of Inco's policies or motives will alter that fact. We sowed, so shall we reap.
The Export Development Corporation loaned Inco $77 million for developing its subsidiary operations in Guatemala and Indonesia. I have heard all the arguments in committee. I have heard all the arguments with respect to the EDC. The Export Development Corporation, I am told by officers of the company, is like a stock record. They say the purpose of the EDC is to encourage and to expedite the export of Canadian prod-
80045-63)4

June 27, 1978
Export Development Act
ucts and services. That basically is the thrust of the Export Development Corporation.
Next we are told that there are certain criteria which govern loans that the EDC makes. First of all is the product viable? Second, is the borrower creditworthy? Third, will the project go ahead? Those are the three criteria on which loans are disbursed by the Export Development Corporation. In the case of Inco's loans, Inco-Guatemala and Inco-Indonesia, one could not doubt that Inco was creditworthy; that is, the parent company. They are creditworthy.
Another criterion was the viability of the project. I have some difficulty as to how the EDC came to the conclusion that the project was a viable one. We have been through this in committee and I will go through it again, again and again until we get through to the people who are responsible for running the Export Development Corporation. Firstly, Inco's operations in Guatemala and Indonesia are lateritic nickel. A lot of energy is needed to smelt lateritic nickel, which is different from the sulphide nickel found in the Sudbury Basin where the ore contains sulphur which acts as an energy agent in reducing the ore. So, in effect, nickel would have to go to $3 a pound before it actually becomes profitable to develop the lateritic nickel of Indonesia and Guatemala. Nickel is now $2.15 a pound. It would have to go to $3 a pound because both those countries have to import a considerable amount of oil at world market prices. That makes the smelting process of that lateritic nickel extremely expensive.
The next step in the game of those corporations operating in Indonesia and Guatemala is to establish a subsidiary in those countries. They then go to the EDC for a loan in order to establish and look for oil so that they can bring that oil on to the market and supply it to their subsidiaries to smelt the nickel. At that point it becomes extremely profitable to exploit those resources. That would have an adverse effect on Canadian nickel and Canadian employment. That is the reality of the situation.
The EDC says that looking at the long term, the project would go ahead anyway. One surely has to set some priorities among the projects for which they have application. Once the money has been loaned, a more advantageous project may come along which does not challenge the Canadian employment picture down the road. The EDC would then not have the money to get into the other project. It is therefore a matter of setting priorities with regard to how the money is loaned.
There must be a sense of responsibility on the part of the Export Development Corporation to ensure that when money is loaned it will not have a disastrous effect on the long-term Canadian employment scene. Does that sound unreasonable? Well, it is not. I have looked at the American version of the Export Development Corporation. I got out the ground rules for the EX-IM Bank in the United States. I want to quote clause 2(B) 1 (B) which governs the activities of the EX-IM Bank:
-in authorizing any loan or guarantee, the Board of Directors shall take into account any serious adverse effect of such loan or guarantee on the competitive position of United States industry, the availability of materials which are in short supply in the United States, and employment in the United States.
It was under that very section that the United States EX-IM Bank turned down an application for a loan from an American steel company to build a steel plant in Trinidad. If you look down the road, you can see that in the long term it would have a disastrous effect in terms of American employment. However, that does not bother the EDC. They are proud to say they made millions of dollars in profit. That is their basic motivation. It would not matter if it were Hitler himself; they would even do business with him.
Indeed, this was taken to the ridiculous when the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce appeared before the committee. I put this example to him. If an automotive parts company in Canada applied for an EDC loan in order to establish a plant in the southern United States, would EDC make the loan, even though it might have a disastrous effect on the automotive industry in that country? The minister replied yes, they would make the loan. That is ridiculous. What is the basis for that? Why are they not farsighted with regard to the way loans are made through EDC?
We have very serious problems. This country accepted over
1,000	refugees from Chile, not because they were being treated properly by that government but because they were put out of the country and living in refugee camps in Argentina, Panama City and Mexico City. When they came to this country, we heard their horror stories. We heard of President Allendc committing suicide by shooting himself with a machine gun 16 times.
Today I picked up a press blurb from the EDC saying they had just completed a loan to Chile of over $40 million. However, we cannot get information on some 1,600 people who are missing. We make a great deal in this House, and quite rightly so, about the dissidents in Russia. We pass Standing Order 43 motions galore. We express a great deal of concern for the plight of dissidents, people who want to leave the Soviet Union to go to Israel. Yet in this situation we have 1,600 people about whom we have no word. We have been promised by the chief of the junta that we will get this information. However, EDC is prepared to lend over $40 million on a long-term basis at very favourable interest rates at the same time as we are accepting refugees from that unfortunate country.
These people have to be checked and questioned. The bureaucrats in our Crown corporations and government departments have become our masters. One would think they are the ones running the country. No one would believe it is the elected members.
This government which goes along with that sort of clothes closet approach is not doing a service to Canada. They should be the first to say this sounds like a reasonable amendment, that EDC should appear every year before a standing committee of the House in order to be questioned by, and be accountable to, parliament. For the minister to stand in his place and

June 27, 1978

offer in exchange for that sort of detailed and extensive appearance and questioning one or two meetings during the estimates period is really an insult to parliament and the people of Canada.
There are very serious problems with the way in which we are lending money. The people of this country are concerned. 1 know those in my constituency are extremely concerned. The fact is that while Inco workers are becoming employed, their government is using their taxes and the credibility of Canada to borrow money in order to lend it to the very people who created the unemployment problem in their area. That is a real slap in the face for them.
The minister also said that EDC loans to companies such as Inco assist third world countries to develop. I say that loans to multinational resource companies do nothing of the sort. In the case of Guatemala, the loan was made to a subsidiary of Inco, a very large and powerful multinational mining company.
Order, please. 1 regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue only with unanimous consent. Does the hon. member have unanimous consent?
Agreed.
No.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the minister has left the chamber. In addition to elaborating on some of the points made by my hon. friend from York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), I wish to correct a few of the remarks the minister contributed to the debate on motion No. 5.
As I understand it, the hon. gentleman said my hon. friend was in error and that there was no need for any reference back to the House because the corporation was always available to the finance committee for examination. I thought the minister had learned more than that during his 20 years in the House. Perhaps we did not teach him very well over here, but, of course, the finance committee has no right to hear from officials of EDC unless there is an appropriation to be voted on, and the stated purpose of this bill is to remove the necessity for the corporation to come back to parliament for more money.
1 wish to advance a few arguments in support of the motion by my hon. friend from York-Simcoe. The first has to do with accountability. The House should know it is the Canadian taxpayer who is eventually responsible for the commitments of the EDC. Despite the fact that the corporation is increasing its borrowing from the private sector, it is the Canadian taxpayer who stands in the breach. Any time the management fails to keep things on a profitable plane it is the Canadian taxpayer who will have to pick up the pieces.
Export Development Act
It is interesting to note that as of April, two months ago, the corporation owed the government SI.3 billion while its loans from outside sources amounted to less than $600 million. When Mr. MacDonald was questioned in the committee about the relationship of EDC to parliament, he said:
We quite frankly stated that we were an agent of the Government of Canada and my presumption is that if this corporation and its board of directors made a mess of it and went bankrupt then the Government of Canada would have to stand behind it.
So there can be no question about where responsibility lies. Because of this situation we say the corporation should be required to come back once a year to account to parliament. The taxpayer, as a co-signer, relies on parliament to protect his interests. If the government wants to extend the corportion's already wide limits, then the voters have a right to expect parliament to insist on accountability by the corporation on an annual basis.
As things rest, everything depends on the judgment of the corporation's management. We are talking about a lot of money. It was disclosed in committee that there is no limitation contemplated other than the statutory ceilings we are talking about in the case of individual deals backed by the corporation. The agency is now in the position of making commitments to the value of $6 billion. There is nothing which would prevent bad judgment on the part of the directors from bankrupting the organization in the event of a bad deal, though I agree this is not likely to happen when there is such a big cushion to rely on.
Mr. MacDonald was asked in the committee whether there was some limit beyond which the corporation would not lend in connection with an individual deal. He replied that there was not. There was no limit beyond which the EDC might go in pledging the credit of the Government of Canada. Mr. Speaker, it is hard to conceive of a corporation which does not operate on the basis of there being some limit governing its deals. Even Citibank has set limits on the size of the loans it makes to other countries, and it is worth noting that Citibank declined to lend Canada more than $175 million in connection with the recent bond issue. We say, therefore, that in the absence of an upper ceiling a regular referral is necessary to enable parliament to keep an adequate watch on what is going on.
Up to this point I have been looking at things from the point of view of the taxpayer. Now, perhaps, we should look at them from the point of view of parliament in relation to the corporation. It is obvious that the EDC has become quite a political animal and that it is incurring criticism from many quarters. It has taken to publicly criticizing in print paid for by its own funds a member of parliament, naming him in local newspapers and in its own newsletter. It has run special advertisements in the Financial Post at a cost of over $20,000 at the same time as this bill was before the House, in addition to running other advertisements in newspapers across Canada.
We must remember that the EDC is a Crown corporation, that it is responsible to parliament and that it should not be

June 27, 1978
Export Development Act
attempting to mobilize political pressure on parliament for its own aims. This question of the accountability of EDC to parliament is critical and central to the amendment proposed by my hon. friend.
I do not wish to take up time unduly but 1 think I must say a few words about the attitude taken by the minister himself-1 see he has returned. I refer to his irresponsible statement earlier, his remark about the committee always having access to officials of EDC, when he should have known that the corporation's affairs cannot be referred to the committee unless there is an appropriation to be voted upon.
It is interesting, too, to note the statement made by the minister accusing the opposition of unduly delaying the progress of this bill. The record will show that the Export Development Corporation first approached the government seeking higher ceilings last October. It took only a month or so for the government to approve new ceilings, but it took five months, until March 20 of this year, before Bill C-36 was brought before the House. So only three months have elapsed, including second reading and days spent on committee hearings, and it seems likely we shall be getting rid of the bill this week.
Better control is needed over a corporation which has a record like that of EDC and which is now asking for such limits. Control is needed over a government which would give such powers and such expansive limits to a corporation which does not have to come to parliament on a regular basis. All the Canadian taxpayer has to rely upon is the promise of the present administration that some future legislation might be coming along this fall. However, if that is the case, we are not quite sure why we have to have this bill before us right now. I urge all hon. members, in the interests of protecting their own voters, if not their own votes, that they should be supporting motion No. 5.

speechtext: I had the impression that motions Nos. 5 and 6 were to be debated and voted on together, but since they are to be debated and voted on separately, the vote on motion No. 5 stands deferred and the House will now proceed to the consideration of motion No. 6 in the name of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez).

Motion No. 6.
That Bill C-36, an act to amend the Export Development Act, be amended by adding immediately after line 34 at page 5 the following new clause:
"7. The corporation shall, before it implements the increase in authority provided by this Act, take into account the effect of such implementation on the Canadian economy and specifically the long and short term effect on employment in Canada."
He said: Mr. Speaker
Dispense.

It is good to see that the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) is in the House tonight. It should be funny.
Let us look at the amendment we have before us. It calls upon the EDC to incorporate a certain criterion before approving a loan. It proposes that the criterion should be that the EDC take into account the long-term and short-term effect on employment. Is that an unreasonable amendment?
I want to reiterate that the EX-IM Bank of the United States is governed by a particular clause which provides that loans issued take into account long-term and short-term effects on employment in the United States. It is difficult for a Canadian worker, whether he works in the pulp and paper industry or in the nickel industry, to see stories about employment being created in his own industry while at the same time he reads in the newspapers that his government has subsidized the company he works for to establish a branch plant operation in a third world country. For him that spells disaster in the long term.
Inco has been granted loans to operate in Guatemala and Indonesia. The EDC claimed it was creating 4,000 man-years of work by lending $77 million to Inco, but Inco laid off 2,300 workers in the Sudbury basin. In the Sudbury basin we do not have an infrastructure around the nickel and copper industries.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext: Not again.
The Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) can say "not again" all she wants, but she knows very well she has problems in her own riding.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
We lost 500 jobs under the NDP.
June 27, 1978

There is unemployment in the minister's riding. Why does she not get out of that government and walk across the floor as her buddy did today? Twenty-three hundred workers were laid off, but the public relations people say
4.000	man-years of employment were created. That was for the short term. In the short-term analysis we have no doubt that with the $77 million loan to Inco the EDC did create
4.000	man-years of work, but it was very high technology and short-term work.
We in the Sudbury basin do not have an infrastructure around the nickel and copper industries. We have no research and development based around that resource. The resource is ripped out of the ground, put in boxcars and shipped out to be processed abroad and then sold back to us as finished products. When any attempt is made by entrepreneurs in the basin to diversify operations, they are told that there is no venture capital for that. No wonder there is not. Our Crown corporation, the EDC, is raising money in Canada's name and lending it to multinational mining companies so that they can go abroad and exploit the resources of third world countries. Much the same was done to us many years ago.
There is a legitimate question in the minds of Canadian workers. As they lose their jobs they see loans being made to the companies they work for. Their companies go abroad, not to develop for the benefit of companies abroad, but for the benefit of themselves.
We have the same situation in the paper industry. I am glad to see that the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi is in the House. The EDC made a loan to Bear Island Paper Company. It is a partnership of Bato Company Incorporated, Dow Jones and Company Limited and the Washington Post Company. That was a loan for $47 million to Virginia for the establishment of a pulp and paper operation. It will be probably one of the most modern plants.
The paper workers there have a concern. They have written to me expressing their concern about the pulp and paper companies in this country which have not modernized their operation so that workers can be more productive. When I was out in Vancouver I found that the MacMillan Bloedel Company's pulp and paper section was decrepit and that their plant needs to be modernized.
In Timiskaming the pulp and paper mill has been closed down. What happened there? EDC has come up with $47 million to develop the pulp and paper industry in the United States which, as EDC has admitted, will be filling markets that are currently being filled by Quebec plants. I just do not see the sense in that sort of operation. Here we have pulp and paper mills in this country having to compete and fill markets, and the EDC is lending money for the long term at favourable interest rates to develop competition for these pulp and paper mills in Canada and moving into the southern United States of all places, which is not noted for modern industrial relations techniques. They have right to work laws on their books, no strike laws on the books, their minimum wage is $2.35 an
Export Development Act
hour, their plants do not have to be heated in the winter and their government gives them years and years of tax free holidays. Those are the hidden realities, but the EDC steps into the breach, as Mr. MacDonald, the president, would say, because "we can make a buck and we are not interested in the long-term effects."
The EDC uses three criteria in making loans. The first is that the plant be creditworthy. Is the operation going to make money? Is it a flexible operation? Will the operation go ahead anyway?

I wonder if I could ask the hon. member a question. Does he honestly believe that if Canadian companies do not participate in the development of the nickel resources in the United States, they would lie undeveloped, or that if Canadian companies which manufacture this mining equipment did not get the business developing in Indonesia or Guatemala, that the great nickel resources in these countries would lie undeveloped? Does he believe that these countries with their rich nickel resources are lying starving and waiting, and that without Canadian participation they would remain undeveloped and in poverty?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member mentioned nickel resources in the United States. He also spoke of Indonesia and Guatemala. It is a good question and I should give the parliamentary secretary credit for asking a good question. Probably he was not in the House when I mentioned the EX-IM Bank because I am always making comparisons. Section 2(B) of the act governing the EX-IM Bank says:
-in authorizing any loan or guarantee, the board of directors shall take into account any serious adverse effect of such loan or guarantee on the competitive position of United States industry, the availability of materials which are in short supply in the United States, and employment in the United States.
It was brought out in committee that in the United States there was an application from a borrower to establish a steel plant in Trinidad. An American company wanted to build that steel plant and it applied to the EX-IM Bank for a loan. The EX-IM Bank considered all the criteria applied by EDC, and in applying the fourth criterion said that to develop the steel plant in Trinidad would, in effect, be competitive and create unemployment in the future among American workers. So the loan was turned down. That does not prevent some other bank, the Japanese equivalent of EDC or the German equivalent, from lending money to build the steel plant in Trinidad.
I am saying to the hon. member that the resources in Guatemala, for example, are not developed by that country, although the impression is left that that is so. I do not know how many times I have to bring this to the attention of the hon. member, but in effect it is an Inco subsidiary that is developing the ore in Guatemala and Indonesia, and it is developing it not for the benefit of the Guatemalan people but for the benefit of the multinational mining company. If Guatemala itself were applying for the loan, then all the criteria would come into effect; that is, the criteria for putting technology into the hands of third world countries and helping them to exert some control over their economic destiny.

June 27, 1978
Export Development Act
But that is not what we have here. We have EDC, promoting imperialism in third world countries, because in effect that resource is being scraped off the top of the ground, put in ships and shipped out to Wales where the final processing is done and the manufacturing of the finished product takes place. It does not take place in Guatemala. So the resource is exploited, but not for the benefit of the people. When the operation is fully operative in Guatemala, only 700 people will be hired. It is a highly capital intensive operation. The labour intensive part of the operation is at the processing and finishing end of the project.
So the suggestion that somehow or other we are helping Indonesia and Guatemala develop their resources through EDC loans is not correct. We are not doing that at all.
Earlier I spoke about pulp and paper mills. We did the same thing with steel plants. One of the things we need to do in Cape Breton is to modernize the steel plant, and it takes a lot of capital to do that. EDC lends millions of dollars to a Canadian company to go down into the United States eastern seaboard to develop a modern steel plant, which makes it very difficult for the Cape Breton steel company to compete for those markets with the kind of decrepid equipment they have and the resulting lack of productivity.
You are comparing apples and oranges.

I am not comparing apples and oranges at all. I would like all these yahoos who are making comments to come up to Nickel Belt, where they will be invited to a public meeting at which 1 would like them to stand up and make all these comments about EDC doing such a great job.
There is also another aspect. The jobs which are created in the short term accrue primarily to the southern part of the province of Ontario. The jobs are created in Toronto and Montreal and some are spun off to Vancouver. Thus, we have the EDC stimulating employment in areas which are already heavily industrialized. For example, if a plant has an order to complete, it will more than likely expand its operation where the original plant is located. So what we have is EDC acting with one set of ground rules while DREE operates with another set of ground rules. Then there is the taxation system which operates with a different set of principles. There is no cohesion whatsoever with respect to the manner in which the loans are given. There is no plan to diversify industrial development into areas which need it.
There is also the question of the effect of employment and the loans of the EDC. In none of the questioning during the EDC committee was there any indication from the officers of that corporation that they even consider the long-term effects on Canadian employment. They are more concerned with showing a good profit. There is also the fact that they do not make moral judgments on the regimes with which they do business.
It seems to me that in this particular instance we should consider the concept-and no one can deny that it is a good

one-that when dealing with Canadian finished products and services there is a good argument to be made for an Export Development Corporation which assembles capital for the export of Canadian finished products. However, when it begins to come into areas where Canada for years has been very predominant, for example the resource sector, it seems to me that it begins to undo whatever good it may have accrued in terms of job creation in the long term.
The taxpayers of this country must be assured that no corporation which they support with their tax money is used to create their unemployment some years down the road. This is what is going to happen. There is no question at all, for example, that when the nickel industry starts coming on stream it will have an adverse effect on the areas dependent on the development of nickel. We cannot get diversification in our areas. We saw today where we would love to have an auto parts plant build some cars and sell them to southern Ontario for a change, but we cannot even get that in the Sudbury Basin. It seems the only strength we have is nickel and copper, so why, if there is money to be loaned, is it not loaned in the Sudbury area so we can diversify our industrial base?
That is a very legitimate question, Mr. Speaker, and a question which people are asking. In spite of the gentle answers and smiles we received in committee, it is a very legitimate question for a man or woman who has worked five years in a nickel or copper mine and who depends on that industry for their income. While the EDC officials may come before the committee and make very esoteric and flim-flammy arguments about how we are, in effect, helping Third World countries and really creating employment, it does not answer the question raised by the Canadian taxpayer who feels the effect of the unemployment created by the loans of the EDC.
I suspect that members opposite will vote against this amendment which we have put before the House. I notice that they are banging their desk tops. That is an indication that they will vote against an eminently wise and judicious amendment. It is obvious they are not concerned about unemployment in this country, particularly the hon. member for Northumberland- Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) who has close to 30 per cent unemployment in his area. He should not be sitting there braying like a donkey; he should be interested in what this amendment says.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is correct when he says the rate of unemployment in my area is high. That is why I have been doing something about it over the last four years. I would not think of braying like a donkey, because I think that is his department.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has been working for four years to improve the 30 per cent unemployment rate since he first came to this House, but it is still 30 per cent. That is work only a Liberal can do, and it is either very bad mathematics or playing around with Canada Works or Young Canada Works grants. I wish that he would participate
June 27, 1978

in the debate on this amendment because it is an extremely important question with respect to his own area where there is pulp and paper industry. The hon. member should be concerned about the effect of that $47 million instead of getting up on spurious points of order. Rather, he should participate in serious debate on how we can make the EDC work for the benefit of Canada, not to the detriment of Canada.
The first and foremost consideration is how this loan will affect employment in Canada in the long term. It is a very wise amendment and I urge hon. members to support it. Let us make the EDC accountable to Canadian taxpayers.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly concerned about this bill and I had hoped that the minister would have given greater consideration to it. This matter was brought to his attention in committee, and it does not seem as though there was very much done about it. Instead, it seems that the government is intent upon supporting business in other countries at the expense of developing our own.
We in Alberta are very concerned about developing our own oil and gas industry. It seems that we will have to do it alone with very little help from the federal government. However, when you consider that the EDC has a line of credit in Algeria of $1.2 billion and we in Alberta are having difficulties developing the petrochemical industry, it is a gross injustice.
I would like to put on the record a quote from The Economist of June 17, 1978 which states that Algeria will spend $28 billion on oil and gas projects between now and 1985, according to a master plan prepared by the American consulting engineers, Bechtel of San Francisco. It will build ten new gas processing plants, six plant extensions, eight reinjection units,
6,000	miles of pipeline, eight gas liquification plants and three oil refineries. The whole oil and gas program will last 30 years. In return Algeria expects to get $250 billion from oil and gas sales over those 30 years.
If those estimates are correct the Algerian government will receive a return of 180 per cent on its investments. It needs every penny of it because 100,000 school leavers will be available on the labour market between 1985 and 2000. By 1993 Algeria plans to sell oil only in its refined state and not as crude.
You can see, Mr. Speaker, that Alberta does have a grudge and 1 hope hon. members opposite recognize this. We want to sell processed gas and build petrochemical plants too. We want to get into the business, but as long as the government insists on helping other countries we will be held back. It is all right, of course, to do this in certain cases, but to do it at the expense of our own country to me is incomprehensible.
The minister comes from Alberta. I hope he will give consideration to the fact that we in Alberta want to get the business too. We do not want to be cast aside because of policies that are hurting us so badly.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, it is the intention to have a vote tonight so I shall continue my remarks on third reading.
Export Development Act

subtopic: ABORTION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF ABORTION LAWS
ABORTION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF ABORTION LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the year 1979 has been designated as the International Year of the Child by the United Nations in commemoration of the signing of the UN declaration on the rights of children some 20 years ago. The purpose of that declaration was to enhance the living standards of children around the world, to improve their nourishment, their education and their total development. All members support that resolution.
On June 9 of this year I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whether he would mark the International Year of the Child in Canada by reviewing Canada's abortion laws. My basic argument at that time was, and still remains, that the greatest gift society can give to a child is, of course, the gift of life. The Prime Minister responded by saying it was not up to the government to give life but rather for God and parents.
Most of us recognize that life is a gift of God, but what I was asking the Prime Minister that day was whether he would review Canada's abortion laws which are removing the right to live inasmuch as they are taking life away from 60,000 Canadian children. The facts before us are a condemnation of each one of us. In 1976 there were 54,536 legal abortions performed in Canada, an increase of 10.4 per cent over the preceding year. It is estimated that an additional 4,000 Canadians had therapeutic abortions performed outside Canada's borders. We know that the figure for the last calendar year exceeds 50,000.
The government has argued that it is not involved in this taking of life by Canada's hospitals and medical personnel who should be dedicated to the preservation of life and the alleviation of suffering. The point is that the government is involved, and it is very directly involved with its grants system.
Planned Parenthood of Canada has largely become an abortion referral agency. More than 90 per cent of its funding comes from federal government grants. The Department of National Health and Welfare has granted $600,000 in the last fiscal year. The Canadian International Development Agency has granted $39,865 in the last year. One might ask whether the purpose of the Canadian International Development Agency is to provide aid to the third world. What is it doing granting aid to Planned Parenthood of Canada?
I could go on, but I know that my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen), will delve into this subject further. However, I want to impress on the government that this blot on society cannot go unchecked any further, because all statistics-and I do not want to speak
8004 5-64 Vi

June 27, 1978
Adjournment Debate
about statistics; I want to speak about people-indicate that legal abortions are increasing on the average by 10 per cent per year.
What is happening to respect for life? What is happening to our civilization? Has life become expendable? All of us have been horrified time after time by pictures of the holocaust of World War II in which life became cheap. I ask sincerely whether we are any different today. If life is expendable for the unborn child, how much longer will it be before life becomes expendable at the other end of the age spectrum? When will society decide to remove life from those who are aged, infirm or terminally ill?
I do not want to play God, but I want to impress upon my colleagues here today-and this subject crosses all political partisan viewpoints-the point that we as a civilization are doomed if we do not respect life. We can have it no other way.
In the study of nations, if one wants to look at comprehensive studies like Arnold Toynbee's from a secular point of view where nations have lost their moral bases and justified everything on the basis of expediency, those nations are doomed.
These are serious words, but I am totally convinced as I stand here that we are going down that road. If we have any respect for life at all, I plead with the government to make the International Year of the Child a year of life and a year in which 60,000 Canadians will not face the spectre of death. I ask the government to reconsider. The Badgley committee stated that if abortions were to continue, the value of life would be lowered. I believe that as a civilization and as a nation we are at the crossroads. I plead with the government to reconsider and to give life to Canada's youngest citizens.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Young (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ABORTION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF ABORTION LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure that I can respond on behalf of the minister to all of the comments of the hon. member this evening. I respect a great number of the points the hon. member has made. One thing I could say on behalf of my minister would be that the federal government would very much like to see an even handed and equally fair administration of the laws of Canada right across the country and throughout each of the provinces. It does not assist us to have our laws interpreted unfairly or differently in the provinces and regions of Canada.
Whereas the abortion provisions fall within the Criminal Code and are a matter of federal jurisdiction, hospitals come under the control and administration of the provinces, and the enforcement of our Criminal Code and the administration of our justice is also under the control of the provinces. Therefore, it is up to the provinces to co-ordinate their approach to and their interpretation of this subject matter.
Without doubt the issue of abortion is a deeply emotional and moral one, and there are bound to be definitive and strongly held feelings on various sides of this issue. It would appear that no matter what words might be used in such a law, their scope will often be determined by the canons of local

medical custom-and those in turn are often set by varying social values in the different regions of this country.
I should point out to the hon. member that my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Robinson), will undoubtedly expand on some of his points and questions in relation to Planned Parenthood, and I understand the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) will also raise some of those points this evening.
I could point out to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) that provision is made in the Criminal Code for provincial ministers of health to review information relating to the circumstances of therapeutic abortions. The justice minister has said that he is not in a position to instruct the provinces on the matter. However, he has stated that he and his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), either directly or through their officials, would be meeting with provincial health officials once those officials have had a thorough opportunity to study the findings of the Badgley report, and the provincial review of the abortion procedure may be one of those topics to be discussed.
I could go on to read some portions of the Badgley report, but 1 think the hon. member is perhaps familiar with them and time will not allow me to do so this evening. Perhaps 1 could discuss this privately with him, if he so wishes.

Mr. Speaker, on June 9 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made one of his cute remarks, which was designed to deflect attention away from the real issues, saying that only God and parents can give life. He said that in partial answer to the question posed to him by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). My question to him was based on the fact that while it is true that only God and parents can give life, it is the abortion clinics which take that life away. I asked the Prime Minister whether or not he would reconsider the policy of this government in funding abortion clinics or groups in society which offer abortion counselling to people and withdraw some of that funding to those organizations.
There are two principles involved in government funding of organizations. Number one, the government has no business funding organizations which have the goal of changing lifestyles. That deals with social programming and programmed responses, and it is a system of robbing citizens of genuine choice.
I have before me the press release of Planned Parenthood Association of British Columbia dated May 16. It says:
The problem is that more babies are being born to those least prepared socially, emotionally or intellectually to function as parents. Many of these disadvan-taged-from-birth children will likely become mentally and physically ill, with a potential for violence that is of serious concern.
June 27, 1978

It appears to me that Planned Parenthood is becoming something omnipotent when they can predict which children- not yet conceived, not yet born-are going to become problems in society. It seems to me that Planned Parenthood is reducing family planning to predetermined choices made by some omnipotent person who decides who has the right to be born. 1 remember a European leader who just 40 years ago decided that only those people who are blond and blue-eyed ought to have the right to bear children.
I hope that this government will not continue to fund organizations which are of that kind of mentality, whether it be different criteria that they use or not. It so happens that my mother had a grade three education and my wife's mother had a grade one education, neither of which were in one of Canada's official languages. I suppose that on the criteria which Planned Parenthood has established neither of those people would have qualified to bear children. My experience with them, however, has been that they were intellectually brilliant people irrespective of their lack of education. That is the first principle, that the government has no business in funding organizations which are determined to change lifestyles.
The second principle is that voluntary organizations must prove broad public support to obtain government funding. If they establish public support by raising money locally, which would indicate that they are enjoying public support, then perhaps the government could examine whether or not the organization deserves broader funding from taxpayers across Canada. The government should fund such organizations only to the extent of matching dollar for dollar.
The kind of budget which Planned Parenthood has established indicates to me that there is no broad public support for that organization. This is indicated by the fact that it could raise only $30,000, while on the other hand it is asking the government to supply $650,000 a year. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) asked the government on April 20 to provide increased funding to Planned Parenthood because they were not keeping up with the cost of living. His rationale was the fact that there were 12,956 teenagers who gave birth in the past year.
There is more education on sex today than ever before. There is less restraint in talking about sex, and there are more teenage pregnancies, but the hon. member for New Westminster or the government presumes that more education will reduce this incidence. The government has no business getting into the funding of organizations which do not enjoy broad public support, and I hope the parliamentary secretary will not bring up the business of how much they give to Serena. That is not the same argument, nor is it the same kind of organization. It is an organization that works for itself.
It seems to me that this whole organization is now deciding that fertility and pregnancy is some kind of disease, that unplanned children or unexpected children are some kind of pestilence on the corporate body. We need to reconstruct our thinking on that. I ask the government again to reconsider their funding policies of Planned Parenthood, to decrease that
Adjournment Debate
funding, and to justify it only on the basis of legitimate family planning and counselling, not on abortion clinics which this organization broadly supports.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that essentially the hon. member's question was the representation that funding in respect of certain groups be withdrawn. I recall that on or about April 6, 1978, I indicated to the hon. member that the Department of National Health and Welfare is attempting to reduce the dependence of these organizations on federal funds. I would point out to the hon. member also that in so far as I am aware the federal government does not provide funds to organizations to change lifestyles. Maybe that is a point upon which the hon. member requires more explanation, but it is not the case.
It may be of assistance to the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) to look back upon the historical development of family planning services and the provisions of the Criminal Code, as well as established programs financing, in order to understand the funding policies of the federal government in this area.
In August 1969, parliament amended the Criminal Code in order to allow for the dissemination of information concerning contraception. In the same year, parliament amended the Criminal Code to allow for therapeutic abortions when, in the opinion of a therapeutic abortion committee, the continuation of pregnancy would or would likely endanger the life or health of the woman.
Following the tabling of the report of the committee on the operation of the abortion law, which stated that most people across Canada from whom information was obtained did not wish to see changes in the law, the federal government indicated that it was not prepared to propose changes in the Criminal Code at the present time.
The Department of National Health and Welfare provides sustaining grants to two national voluntary agencies, namely Serena Canada and the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada, in accordance with their objective of providing family planning services and information on all contraceptive means. These agencies received $175,000 and $600,000 respectively, based on the extent of their activities in the area I mentioned. The department does not fund agencies whose activities are predominantly directed towards implementing changes in Canadian law, nor does it align itself with either the pro-abortion or anti-abortion positions.
On September 11, 1973, the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde), the former minister of national health and welfare, stated:
In terms of general policy, the federal government does not regard abortion as an acceptable method of birth control; I should like that point to be made very clear. It does, however, recognize that unwanted conceptions may occur as a result of failure to use an effective method of contraception or any contraception at all. In these cases, there may be justification for therapeutic abortion, not because the pregnancy was unplanned but because it may have given rise to

June 27, 1978
Adjournment Debate
conditions which, in the opinion of a therapeutic abortion committee, provide appropriate grounds for termination in accordance with the Criminal Code.
The minister went on to say:
Birth control clinics are often visited by women seeking advice about unwanted pregnancies. To turn them away without help would be inhumane and could be regarded as tantamount to an attempt by the clinic's staff to impose their personal views about a subject on which society has expressed its collective will through the law.
On March 4, 1977, he also announced that the federal government would work with provincial governments to ensure that family planning services are made available to all those who wish to use them, and at the same time would intensify its own planning information program.
